bank.question: In IALA Region A, what are the standard colors and shapes for port and starboard lateral marks when entering a harbour in the direction of buoyage?
bank.explanation: Under IALA Region A, lateral port hand marks are red cans and starboard hand marks are green cones
options: Green cones and red cans
Red cans and green cones
Red cones and green cans
Black pillars and yellow spars

bank.question: Which VHF signal is used to announce a message concerning the safety of navigation or important meteorological warnings?
bank.explanation: A 'Securite' signal is used to broadcast important meteorological warnings or navigational safety information, such as a buoy out of position or a drifting log
options: Mayday
Pan Pan
Securite
Distress Alert

bank.question: Which topmark correctly identifies an East Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: East Cardinal marks have two cones pointing away from each other (base to base). Pass to the East of this mark for safe water.
options: Two cones pointing away from each other (base to base).
Two cones pointing towards each other (point to point).
A single sphere.
A single cone pointing upwards.

bank.question: What is an 'Occulting' light?
bank.explanation: An oculting light is a light where the total duration of light in each period is longer than the total duration of darkness (the light is 'on' more than it is 'off')
options: A light where the duration of light is longer than the duration of darkness
A light where the duration of darkness is longer than the duration of light
A light that flashes exactly once every ten seconds
A light that changes colour from red to green

bank.question: In navigation, what does the term 'Variation' refer to?
bank.explanation: Variation is the angular difference between Magnetic North and True North, caused by the Earth's magnetic field
options: The angle between Magnetic North and a ship's compass North
The difference between a back-bearing and a forward bearing
The angular difference between True North and Magnetic North
The movement of the tide over a 6 hour period

bank.question: Which lights must a vessel 'Not Under Command' show at night when making no way through the water?
bank.explanation: A vessel 'not under command' (due to exceptional circumstances like engine failure) must show two all-round red lights in a vertical line at night
options: Three all-round red lights in a vertical line
One all-round green light over one all-round white light
Two all-round white lights in a vertical line
Two all-round red lights in a vertical line

bank.question: What is the purpose of a 'Clearing Bearing' in navigation?
bank.explanation: A clearing bearing is a pre-planned line on a chart that ensures a vessel stays clear of a specific hazard, such as a submerged rock or shallow bank.
options: To provide a precise line for a vessel to follow into a harbour.
To ensure a vessel stays clear of a specific hazard, such as a submerged rock or shallow bank.
To determine the vessel's speed over ground.
To indicate the direction of the strongest tidal flow.

bank.question: In pilotage, what is a 'Transit'?
bank.explanation: A Transit occurs when two fixed objects are observed to be in line, providing a highly accurate position line
options: A bearing taken with a hand-bearing compass
A line drawn on the chart towards a single landmark
Two fixed objects observed to be in a line
The path a vessel takes when crossing a shipping lane

bank.question: According to COLREGs Rule 5, when must a vessel maintain a proper look-out?
bank.explanation: Rule 5 of COLREGs states that every vessel shall at all times maintain a proper look-out by sight and hearing as well as by all available means
options: Only at night or in restricted visibility
At all times, by sight, hearing, and all available means
Only when navigating in busy shipping lanes
Whenever the skipper is below deck

bank.question: When do 'Neap Tides' occur?
bank.explanation: Neap tides occur during the first and third quarters of the moon, resulting in a smaller tidal range
options: When the moon is at its first or third quarter
When the moon is new or full
When the sun and moon are in alignment with the Earth
When the sun is at its furthest point from the equator

bank.question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel is the 'Give-Way' vessel according to ColRegs Rule 15?
bank.explanation: Under ColRegs Rule 15, when two power-driven vessels are crossing, the vessel which has the other on her own starboard side must keep out of the way.
options: The vessel on the port side of the other vessel.
The vessel which has the other on her own port side.
The vessel which has the other on her own starboard side.
The vessel that is going faster.

bank.question: What is the light characteristic of an East Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: A quick-flashing white light (either 3 flashes every 5 or 10 seconds) identifies a East Cardinal mark
options: Two flashes every 5 seconds
Three flashes every 5 or 10 seconds
Six flashes plus one long flash
Continuous quick flashing

bank.question: When do 'Neap' tides typically occur?
bank.explanation: Neap tides occur when the moon is at its first or last quarter, resulting in the smallest tidal range
options: At the first and last quarter moon
During a full moon or new moon
Only during the summer solstice
When the sun and moon are in direct alignment with Earth

bank.question: According to COLREGs, which vessel is the stand-on vessel when one vessel is overtaking another?
bank.explanation: Rule 13 states that an overtaking vessel must keep well clear of the vessel being overtaken
options: The vessel to starboard has right of way
The larger vessel has right of way
The vessel being overtaken must alter course to starboard
The overtaking vessel must keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken

bank.question: Which of the following describes an 'Occulting' light characteristic?
bank.explanation: An occulting light is a rhythmic light in which the total duration of light in each period is longer than the total duration of darkness.
options: A light that flashes at regular intervals, but with a longer period of darkness than light.
A light that has a total duration of light in each period longer than the total duration of darkness.
A light that shows a continuous light with no interruptions.
A light that rapidly flashes five times followed by a longer flash.

bank.question: What is the shape and colour of a Starboard Hand lateral mark in IALA Region A?
bank.explanation: In IALA Region A, the Starboard Hand mark is green with a conical/triangular topmark
options: Red pillar with a square topmark
Green buoy with a cone or triangle topmark
Green buoy with a cylinder or can topmark
Yellow and black buoy with a diamond topmark

bank.question: What characterizes 'Spring' tides?
bank.explanation: Spring tides feature the highest high waters and lowest low waters, creating the greatest range
options: High water is lower than average and low water is higher than average
The time between high and low water is shorter than 6 hours
The tidal range is at its minimum
High water is at its highest and low water at its lowest

bank.question: Two sailing vessels are approaching each other on opposite tacks. Which vessel is the stand-on vessel?
bank.explanation: A Close-Hauled sailing vessel on Port tack must give way to a sailing vessel on Starboard tack
options: The vessel to leeward
The vessel on Port tack
The vessel on Starboard tack
The faster vessel

bank.question: When entering a UK harbour in the direction of the flood tide, what are the characteristics of a Port Hand lateral mark?
bank.explanation: In IALA Region A (UK), the Port hand lateral mark is red with a cylindrical (can) topmark.
options: It is green with a conical topmark.
It is red with a spherical topmark.
It is red with a cylindrical (can) topmark.
It is green with a cylindrical (can) topmark.

bank.question: Which VHF channel is used for initial distress calls and calling other stations?
bank.explanation: CH 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling channel
options: Channel 16
Channel 06
Channel 70
Channel 12

bank.question: If the charted depth is 2.5m and the height of tide is 3.0m, what is the actual depth of water?
bank.explanation: To calculate Depth, add the Height of Tide to the Charted Datum Depth. Height of tide (3.0m) + Charted depth (2.5m) = 5.5m

bank.question: How do you calculate the height of tide for a 'Secondary Port'?
bank.explanation: Standard Port heights are found in tide tables; secondary port heights are calculated using time and height differences
options: Read it directly from the Chart Datum
Subtract the drying height from the depth
Check the local GPS data for the previous day
Apply time and height differences to a Standard Port

bank.question: Which description correctly identifies a West Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: A West Cardinal mark has topmark cones pointing 'in' towards each other and a yellow band in the middle of a black body. It indicates that safe water lies to the West of the mark.
options: Topmark cones pointing away from each other (base to base) and a yellow band in the middle of a black body.
Topmark cones pointing 'in' towards each other, a yellow band in the middle of a black body, and indicates safe water to the West.
Topmark cones pointing 'in' towards each other, a black band in the middle of a yellow body, and indicates safe water to the East.
A black body with a single red horizontal band and two black spheres as a topmark.

bank.question: What weather sequence is typically associated with the approach of a Warm Front?
bank.explanation: A warm front is typically preceded by a gradual thickening of clouds and steady, prolonged rain
options: Sudden heavy showers and thunderstorms
A period of steady rain and a rise in temperature
Clear blue skies and dropping temperatures
Dense fog and decreasing wind speeds

bank.question: When encountering a North Cardinal Mark, where is the safest water located?
bank.explanation: Cardinal marks indicate the side of the buoy on which the safest water lies; a North mark means safe water is to the North
options: To the North of the mark
To the South of the mark
Passed closely on either side
Inside the nearest harbour

bank.question: What does the term 'Lee Shore' mean?
bank.explanation: Lee Shore refers to the shore towards which the wind is blowing, posing a danger of grounding
options: The shore that is protected from the wind
The shore towards which the wind is blowing
The shore from which the wind is blowing
The coastal area filtered by a mountain range

bank.question: Which buoy marks a hazard of limited size that has navigable water all around it?
bank.explanation: An isolated danger mark is black with one or more red horizontal bands and two black spheres as a topmark.
options: A red cylindrical buoy with a can topmark.
A green conical buoy with a cone topmark.
A black buoy with one or more red horizontal bands and two black spheres as a topmark.
A yellow buoy with a spherical topmark.

bank.question: What are the colours of a 'Safe Water Mark'?
bank.explanation: A safe-water mark has vertical red and white stripes and a single red sphere topmark
options: Red and white vertical stripes
Red and black horizontal stripes
Yellow and black horizontal stripes
All red with a white horizontal band

bank.question: What is meant by the navigational term 'Course to Steer' (CTS)?
bank.explanation: The 'course to steer' must account for the offset caused by the tidal stream (Set and Drift)
options: The compass heading ignoring tide
The direction the boat must head to counteract tide and leeway to reach a destination
The actual path the boat has travelled over the ground
The bearing of the destination from the starting point

bank.question: What prefix is used for a VHF radio message concerning an urgent safety problem that is not life-threatening?
bank.explanation: A 'Pan-Pan' call is used for urgent situations regarding safety that do not constitute an immediate danger to life or the vessel
options: Mayday
Securite
Pan-Pan
Urgency

bank.question: In a Course To Steer (CTS) diagram, what does the Course To Steer represent?
bank.explanation: The Course To Steer (CTS) is the heading the vessel must point to counteract the tide and wind (leeway) to achieve the intended Ground Track.
options: The actual path the vessel makes over the ground.
The direction and speed of the tidal current.
The vessel's Water Track, which is the heading the boat is steered through the water to counteract tide and wind.
The desired destination of the vessel.

bank.question: What describes 'Spring Tides'?
bank.explanation: Spring tides occur when the Gravitational pull of the Sun and Moon are in alignment, resulting in the greatest tidal range
options: The period of lowest high tides
Tides that occur during the first and third quarter of the moon
Tides with the greatest range between high and low water
Tides that occur only during the winter months

bank.question: What day shape must a sailing vessel display when it is being propelled by machinery?
bank.explanation: A sailing vessel under engine power is considered a power-driven vessel and must display a cone, apex down
options: A ball
A cylinder
A cone, apex down
A diamond

bank.question: In navigation, what is the definition of 'Variation'?
bank.explanation: Variation is the angle between True North and Magnetic North, caused by the Earth's magnetic poles not aligning with its geographic poles
options: The difference between True North and Magnetic North
The error caused by magnetic influences on the individual boat
The change in tide height over an hour
The difference between the magnetic heading and the ship's compass reading

bank.question: According to ColRegs Rule 15, in a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel is the 'Stand-on' vessel?
bank.explanation: According to ColRegs Rule 15, when two power-driven vessels are crossing, the vessel which has the other on her own starboard side shall keep out of the way. Therefore, the vessel which sees the other on her own port side is the stand-on vessel.
options: The vessel that sees the other on her own starboard side.
The vessel that is to the port side of the other vessel.
The vessel that has the other on her own starboard side.
The vessel that sounds a prolonged blast.

bank.question: What is the light characteristic of a South Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: A South Cardinal mark features two downward-pointing cones and flashes 6 quick (or ultra-quick) flashes followed by one long flash
options: 3 Quick flashes every 10 seconds
6 Quick flashes followed by 1 long flash
A continuous stream of quick flashes
9 Quick flashes every 15 seconds

bank.question: Which of the following barometric pressure readings is most likely to indicate settled, fair weather?
bank.explanation: A standard barometer reading for fair, settled weather is 1013 hPa; values significantly higher indicate high pressure
options: 980 HPa
995 HPa
1000 HPa
1020 HPa

bank.question: According to COLREGs, what action should two power-driven vessels take when meeting head-on?
bank.explanation: Under COLREGs Rule 14, when two power-driven vessels are meeting on reciprocal courses, both must alter course to starboard to pass port-to-port
options: The larger vessel stands on while the smaller vessel alters to port
Both vessels must stop and wait for a VHF communication
Both vessels should alter course to port to pass starboard-to-starboard
Both vessels should alter course to starboard to pass port-to-port

bank.question: When using a 'Transit' or 'Leading Line' to stay in a deep water channel, what is the role of the 'front mark'?
bank.explanation: A Transit (or Leading Line) uses two fixed objects aligned in a row to provide a highly accurate position line; in this case, the tower and the chimney. The front mark is the object closest to the observer.
options: It is the object furthest from the observer, used to establish depth.
It is the object closest to the observer, which, when aligned with the back mark, provides a precise position line.
It indicates the direction of the prevailing wind.
It acts as a warning for submerged hazards.

bank.question: What does the term 'Veering' mean in a weather forecast?
bank.explanation: Veering refers to a wind shift in a clockwise direction (e.g., South to South-West). Backing is anti-clockwise
options: The wind shifting in an anti-clockwise direction
The wind shifting in a clockwise direction
A sudden increase in wind speed without a change in direction
The wind decreasing in strength significantly

bank.question: In meteorology, what does it mean when the wind 'backs'?
bank.explanation: A backing wind shifts in an anti-clockwise direction (e.g., North to North-West)
options: The wind shifts in a clockwise direction
The wind shifts in an anti-clockwise direction
The wind speed increases suddenly
The wind speed drops to zero

bank.question: What day shape must a vessel 'Restricted in her Ability to Manoeuvre' display?
bank.explanation: Vessels restricted in their ability to manoeuvre (due to the nature of their work) must show a ball-diamond-ball shape by day
options: Three black balls in a vertical line
A single black cylinder
A black ball, a black diamond, and a black ball in a vertical line
Two black diamonds in a vertical line

bank.question: You want to leave a pontoon by 'springing the bow off' using slow ahead gear and fenders. Which mooring line must remain attached to act as the pivot point?
bank.explanation: The aft spring prevents the vessel from moving forward while the engine is in gear, allowing the bow to swing out away from the pontoon.
options: Aft spring
Forward breastline
Aft breastline
Bow line

bank.question: In tidal navigation, what does the term 'Set' refer to?
bank.explanation: The 'Set' is the compass direction towards which a tidal stream or current is flowing. 'Drift' is the speed
options: The speed at which the tide is moving
The direction towards which the tidal stream is flowing
The total distance the boat has been pushed off course
The direction from which the wind is blowing

bank.question: According to COLREGs, if two power-driven vessels are meeting on nearly reciprocal courses so as to involve risk of collision, what action should they take?
bank.explanation: Under Rule 14, when two power-driven vessels meet on reciprocal courses, both must alter course to starboard
options: Both vessels should alter course to starboard
Both vessels should alter course to port
The larger vessel has right of way
The vessel with the wind on its port side stands on

bank.question: What is the topmark for an 'Isolated Danger' mark?
bank.explanation: An Isolated Danger mark is placed directly over a hazard and is identified by two black spheres as its topmark
options: Two black spheres
A single red can
A yellow cross
Two black cones pointing towards each other

bank.question: You are navigating near a dangerous sandbank. The chart indicates that safe water is to the South of the hazard. Which buoy should you look for?
bank.explanation: A South Cardinal mark has two downward-pointing cones as its topmark and a yellow-over-black colour sequence on the buoy body.
options: A South Cardinal mark
An East Cardinal mark
A Lateral mark (starboard hand)
An Isolated Danger mark

bank.question: How do you calculate the time and height of high water for a 'Secondary Port'?
bank.explanation: Standard Port data is found in the main tide tables; Secondary Port heights are calculated by applying time and height differences to a Standard Port
options: By adding 2 metres to the nearest Standard Port high water
By looking at the primary curve on the GPS chartplotter only
By applying time and height differences to the data of a linked Standard Port
By subtracting the mean sea level from the charted depth

bank.question: When entering a harbor in IALA Region A, what are the characteristics of a 'Preferred Channel to Starboard' mark?
bank.explanation: In IALA Region A, the preferred channel to starboard mark is a red can shape with a horizontal green band
options: Green buoy, conical shape, with a red band
Red buoy, cylindrical shape, with a green band
Green buoy, conical shape, with a single light flash
Red buoy, conical shape, with a green band

bank.question: What is meant by a 'Group Flashing' light?
bank.explanation: A 'Grouping' light characteristic (e.g., Fl (2)) means the light shows a specific number of flashes in a repeating pattern
options: The light is only visible from a specific sector
The light changes colour every five seconds
The light stays on for longer than it is dark
The flashes are delivered in a specific number or group

bank.question: You are navigating around a hazard. Which of these describes a North Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: A North Cardinal mark has two cones pointing upwards and indicates that the safest water is to the North of the buoy.
options: Two cones pointing upwards
Two cones pointing downwards
Two spheres
A single upright cone

bank.question: What is an 'Isobar'?
bank.explanation: An 'Isobar' is a line on a weather map (synoptic chart) connecting points of equal atmospheric pressure
options: A line on a weather map connecting points of equal barometric pressure
A line showing the predicted path of a tropical depression
A tool used to measure the humidity in the air
The boundary between two different air masses

bank.question: Under COLREGs, a sailing vessel is overtaking a power-driven vessel from a direction more than 22.5 degrees abaft her beam. Which vessel is the give-way vessel?
bank.explanation: Rule 13 states that any vessel overtaking any other shall keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken
options: The sailing vessel, as the overtaking vessel, must keep clear
The power-driven vessel, because sail gives way to power when overtaking
The power-driven vessel, because it is more maneuverable
Both vessels must alter course to starboard to pass port-to-port

bank.question: Which lights may a power-driven vessel of less than 12 metres in length show as an alternative to the standard configuration?
bank.explanation: A power-driven vessel under 12m may display an all-round white light and sidelights instead of separate steaming and stern lights
options: Two red lights in a vertical line
An all-round white light and sidelights
One yellow flashing light and a green sidelight
A single white light only, even if sidelights are missing

bank.question: A 'Dead Reckoning' (DR) position is calculated using only your course steered and distance through the water. How is it typically represented on a chart?
bank.explanation: A Dead Reckoning (DR) position is calculated using only your course steered and distance through the water, marked on a chart with a single line across the track.
options: With a single line across the track
With a circle around the intersection of position lines
With an arrow pointing to the vessel's estimated position
With a square symbol

bank.question: In a weather forecast, what does the term 'Backing' mean?
bank.explanation: A Backing wind changes direction anti-clockwise (e.g., North to North-West), whereas Veering is clockwise
options: A wind that changes direction clockwise
A wind that changes direction anti-clockwise
A wind that increases in strength quickly
A wind that remains constant but drops in temperature

bank.question: What are the day mark and colour characteristics of a South Cardinal Mark?
bank.explanation: A South Cardinal Mark has two downward-pointing black cones and a yellow-over-black colour scheme
options: Top cones pointing towards each other, black band in the middle
Top cones pointing away from each other, yellow band in the middle
Two cones pointing downwards, black band on the bottom half
Two cones pointing upwards, black band on the top half

bank.question: A power-driven vessel is overtaking a sailing vessel from two points abaft the beam. Which vessel must keep clear?
bank.explanation: Standard Rule 13 states an overtaking vessel must keep clear of the vessel being overtaken, regardless of sail or power
options: The overtaking vessel must keep clear
The sailing vessel always has right of way over power
The vessel to starboard has right of way
The faster vessel is the stand-on vessel

bank.question: You are departing a pontoon and want to 'spring the stern out' using slow astern gear. Which line should you use?
bank.explanation: To spring the stern out from a pontoon while in reverse gear, you should use a stern spring to hold the aft part of the boat while the bow swings out.
options: Stern spring
Bow line
Forward breastline
Aft breastline

bank.question: From which level are 'Drying Heights' on a nautical chart measured?
bank.explanation: Drying heights are measured from the Chart Datum upwards to the seabed. Above LAT (the datum), objects dry at low tide
options: The Highest Astronomical Tide (HAT)
Mean High Water Springs (MHWS)
Chart Datum (CD)
Mean Low Water Neaps (MLWN)

bank.question: What is the primary difference between 'Variation' and 'Deviation' in magnetic navigation?
bank.explanation: Variation is the angle between True North and Magnetic North, caused by the Earth's magnetic fields. Deviation is caused by local onboard magnetism
options: Variation is fixed; Deviation changes hourly
Variation is caused by the engine; Deviation is caused by the Earth's poles
Variation is local to the boat; Deviation is the same for all boats in the area
Variation is caused by the Earth's magnetic field; Deviation is caused by magnetic influences on the boat

bank.question: What is the topmark and light characteristic of a North Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: A North Cardinal mark has two cones pointing upwards and flashes continuously (white light)
options: Two cones pointing down; 6 quick flashes + 1 long flash
Two cones pointing up; continuous quick or very quick flashes
Two cones pointing towards each other; 9 quick flashes
Two cones pointing away from each other; 3 quick flashes

bank.question: You see a vessel at night displaying lights. Which configuration indicates a vessel 'Not Under Command' (NUC)?
bank.explanation: Under IRPCS Rule 27, a vessel 'Not Under Command' shows two all-round red lights in a vertical line when making way at night.
options: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line
A red light over a white light
Two red lights with a white light between them
Three white lights in a vertical line

bank.question: In navigation, what does the term 'Drift' refer to in relation to tidal streams?
bank.explanation: Drift is the speed of the tidal stream, whereas 'Set' is the direction in which the tide is flowing
options: The direction the tide is flowing towards
The distance the vessel has travelled over ground
The difference between Magnetic and True North
The speed of the tidal stream

bank.question: In tidal theory, what is the 'Rule of Twelfths' used for?
bank.explanation: The Rule of Twelfths is a rule of thumb used to estimate the height of tide at hourly intervals between high and low water
options: To calculate the distance to the horizon at different eye heights
To estimate the hourly change in tidal height during a 6-hour cycle
To determine the speed of a tidal stream in a narrow channel
To calculate the safety clearance under a bridge at high water

bank.question: What day shape must a vessel display when at anchor during daylight hours?
bank.explanation: A black ball is the universal day shape for a vessel at anchor (Rule 30)
options: One black ball
Two black balls in a vertical line
A black cone pointing downwards
A black cylinder

bank.question: You are moored port-side to a pontoon and wish to spring the bow off using 'Slow Ahead' power. Which line is the Aft Spring?
bank.explanation: The aft spring runs from the stern of the boat forward to the pontoon, preventing the vessel from moving ahead while in gear.
options: The line running from the stern of the boat forward to the pontoon
The line running from the bow of the boat forward to the pontoon
The line running perpendicular from the bow to the pontoon
The line running perpendicularly from the stern to the pontoon

bank.question: What is the definition of 'Magnetic Deviation'?
bank.explanation: Deviation is the error caused by local magnetic fields on the individual boat, such as engine blocks or electronics
options: The angle between True North and Magnetic North
The error caused by the rotation of the Earth
The error caused by local magnetic fields on the vessel
The difference between your heading and your track

bank.question: Which weather conditions are most commonly associated with the approach of a Warm Front?
bank.explanation: A warm front is typically associated with a lowering of cloud base (stratus) and the onset of steady, persistent rain
options: Low cloud and steady, persistent rain
Clear skies and sudden, heavy squalls
Rapidly rising pressure and bright sunshine
Fog followed by a sudden drop in temperature

bank.question: When using the 'Rule of Twelfths', what proportion of the tide is estimated to rise during the third hour?
bank.explanation: The 1 in 12 rule approximates the tidal rise: 1/12 in the 1st hour, 2/12 in the 2nd, 3/12 in the 3rd and 4th, 2/12 in the 5th, and 1/12 in the 6th

bank.question: What is the topmark used for an Isolated Danger Mark?
bank.explanation: The Isolated Danger mark features two black spheres as a topmark and is placed directly over a hazard that has navigable water all around it.
options: Two black spheres
Two cones pointing upwards
A single red sphere
A single black cone

bank.question: What is a 'Depression' in meteorological terms?
bank.explanation: Warm air is less dense and creates lower pressure; the weight of the atmosphere is lower at the surface
options: A region of low atmospheric pressure
A region of high atmospheric pressure
A fast-moving cold front
A period of calm, clear weather

bank.question: What two primary pieces of information are used to plot a 'Dead Reckoning' (DR) position?
bank.explanation: Dead Reckoning (DR) only uses the course steered and the distance through the water, ignoring external factors like tide
options: Course Steered, Distance through water, and Tidal Stream
Ground Track, Leeway, and Tide Flow
Course Steered and Distance through water only
Compass Heading and Depth Soundings

bank.question: According to COLREGs, what is the colour and arc of visibility of a stern light?
bank.explanation: The Transom (stern) light must be white and have an arc of 135 degrees
options: Yellow; 135 degrees
White; 112.5 degrees
Red; 22.5 degrees
White; 135 degrees

bank.question: After taking two bearings with a hand-bearing compass, you have plotted your position. Which symbol represents a 'Fix'?
bank.explanation: A 'Fix' is represented on a chart by the intersection of position lines, usually identified by a circle around the intersection or a cross with the time written beside it.
options: A circle around the intersection of position lines or a cross with the time written beside it
A single line crossing the vessel's track
A square symbol with the time written inside
A dashed line indicating an estimated position

bank.question: What two factors are used to plot a 'Dead Reckoning' (DR) position?
bank.explanation: A Dead Reckoning (DR) position uses only the course steered and the distance through the water (log), ignoring tide and leeway
options: Course steered and Speed Over Ground (SOG)
Ground track and Tidal Set
Course steered and distance through the water (Log)
Estimated Position (EP) adjusted for Leeway

bank.question: On a chart, if a port hand lateral mark is described as 'Fl(2) R 6s', what light pattern should you expect to see?
bank.explanation: Standard Port marks (Red) emit flashes in even numbers (e.g., 2, 4, 6), whereas Starboard marks (Green) emit odd numbers
options: A single long flash every 10 seconds
A continuous quick flashing light
An odd number of green flashes
An even number of red flashes

bank.question: If your True course is 180 degreesT and the Variation is 7 degreesW, what is the Magnetic course?
bank.explanation: To find Magnetic from True, you ADD West Variation (Error West, Compass Best). 180 + 7 = 187
options: 187 DegreesM
173 DegreesM
180 DegreesM
194 DegreesM

bank.question: You are navigating at night and see lights ahead. Which light configuration indicates a vessel 'Engaged in Trawling'?
bank.explanation: A trawler displays green over white 'all-round' lights, while a vessel engaged in fishing other than trawling displays red over white.
options: Green over white all-round lights
Red over white all-round lights
Two red all-round lights in a vertical line
White over red all-round lights

bank.question: Under COLREGs, what is the primary responsibility of a 'stand-on' vessel when in a potential collision situation?
bank.explanation: Under COLREGs, the stand-on vessel should maintain her course and speed to allow the give-way vessel to take action
options: Change course to port immediately
Maintain course and speed
Stop the engine and wait
Sound five short blasts and turn to starboard

bank.question: Where must a 'Tricolour' light be positioned on a sailing vessel under 20 metres?
bank.explanation: Rule 25 states that a sailing vessel under 20m in length may use a combined 'tricolour' lantern at the top of the mast
options: At the bow, below the pulpit
At or near the top of the mast where it can best be seen
On the stern, alongside the white light
On the spreader, at least 1 metre below the masthead

bank.question: What is the topmark and light characteristic of a South Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: A South Cardinal mark features two cones pointing downwards and flashes in groups of 6 plus one long flash
options: Two cones with points downwards (6 quick flashes + 1 long flash)
Two cones with points upwards (Continuous quick flashing)
Two cones with bases together (9 quick flashes)
Two cones with points together (3 quick flashes)

bank.question: Which channel is the internationally recognised hailing and distress frequency for routine initial calls or monitoring for distress signals?
bank.explanation: Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency used for initial contact before moving to a working channel.
options: Channel 16
Channel 68
Channel 70
Channel 72

bank.question: How is the total depth of water calculated for a specific time and location?
bank.explanation: To find the depth at a specific time, you add the predicted height of the tide to the charted depth foundations
options: Minimum Depth + Charted Depth
Height of Tide - Drying Height
Charted Depth + Height of Tide
Drying Height + Height of Tide

bank.question: Which VHF channel is used for the initial call during a Mayday or Pan-Pan distress situation?
bank.explanation: CH 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling channel; it must be monitored at all times while at sea
options: VHF Channel 16
VHF Channel 06
VHF Channel 13
VHF Channel 67

bank.question: What weather conditions are typically associated with a rising barometer and high pressure?
bank.explanation: A steady or rising barometer usually indicates the approach or presence of a high-pressure system (Anticyclone)
options: Strong winds and heavy rain
A rapid drop in temperature
The arrival of a Cold Front
Settled weather and light winds

bank.question: When plotting an Estimated Position (EP) and accounting for the wind's effect on the hull, which vector represents 'Leeway'?
bank.explanation: The Leeway vector is applied to the Water Track (the direction the boat is pointed) to account for the wind pushing the vessel sideways.
options: The vector applied to the Water Track to account for sideways wind push
The vector indicating the boat's speed through the water
The vector representing the current's effect on the boat
The vector for the boat's intended direction over ground

bank.question: What is the definition of an 'Estimated Position' (EP)?
bank.explanation: The Estimated Position (EP) is the most accurate plot as it accounts for both the vessel's movement and environmental factors like tide and wind
options: A position excluding tidal flow
A DR position adjusted for Tide (Set and Drift) and Leeway
A position obtained using three visual bearings only
A position based solely on speed through the water and time

bank.question: How is the 'Height of Tide' defined in UK Admiralty tide tables?
bank.explanation: Height of tide is measured from the Chart Datum (CD), which is usually the Lowest Astronomical Tide level
options: From the seabed to the surface
From Mean High Water Springs to the surface
From Chart Datum (CD) to the water surface
From the yacht's keel to the seabed

bank.question: What is the minimum requirement for navigation lights for a power-driven vessel of less than 12 metres in length?
bank.explanation: Vessels under 12m length may display an all-round white light and sidelights if they cannot fit the standard configuration
options: An all-round white light and sidelights
A single yellow flashing light
Two red lights in a vertical line
Sidelights only with no white lights

bank.question: Which topmark identifies a 'Safe Water Mark' when approaching a landfall after a cross-channel passage?
bank.explanation: The Safe Water Mark is identified by a single red sphere topmark and vertical red and white stripes on the body.
options: A single red sphere
Two black cones pointing upwards
Two black cones pointing away from each other
A single green can

bank.question: From what level are chartered soundings (depths) measured?
bank.explanation: On UK Admiralty charts, depths are measured from Chart Datum, which is usually the 'Lowest Astronomical Tide' (LAT)
options: Mean High Water Springs (MHWS)
Mean Sea Level (MSL)
Chart Datum (LAT)
Mean Low Water Neaps (MLWN)

bank.question: What is the topmark of an 'Isolated Danger' mark?
bank.explanation: Isolated Danger Marks are placed directly over a hazard and are identified by two black spheres as a topmark
options: A single red sphere
Two black spheres
A yellow 'X' shape
A single black cone pointing upwards

bank.question: Which light combination is shown by a vessel engaged on pilotage duty?
bank.explanation: A pilot boat on duty displays white over red lights ('White hat, red nose')
options: Red over White
White over Red
Green over White
Red over Red over Red

bank.question: As a look-out at night, you see a single white light directly ahead, which you confirm is not a steaming light. Which light indicates you are the 'Overtaking' vessel?
bank.explanation: A vessel is deemed to be overtaking when approaching another from a direction more than 22.5 degrees abaft her beam, where only the stern light would be visible.
options: A single white stern light
A white masthead light with side lights
A single flashing yellow light
Two vertical white lights

bank.question: According to the 'Rule of Twelfths', how much of the tidal range rises or falls during the fourth hour?
bank.explanation: In the 'Rule of Twelfths', the tide rises/falls by 1/12 in the first hour, 2/12 in the second, and 3/12 in the third and fourth
options: 2/12Ths
1/6Th
3/12Ths

bank.question: In navigation, how is an 'Estimated Position' (EP) derived?
bank.explanation: The 'Estimated Position' (EP) is the best guess of a boat's position, calculated by applying the estimated effect of tidal stream and leeway to a Dead Reckoning (DR)
options: The vessel's position according to GPS coordinates
Directly applying the effect of tide and leeway to a Dead Reckoning (DR) position
The position of the vessel if no wind or current were present
The location of the nearest safe haven or port of refuge

bank.question: In navigation, what does the term 'Leeway' describe?
bank.explanation: Leeway is the leeward (downwind) drift of a vessel caused by the wind pushing against the hull and rigging
options: The sideways drift of a vessel caused by the wind
The distance a vessel travels over the ground
The effect of the tidal stream on the hull
The difference between magnetic and true north

bank.question: When entering a UK harbour at night, which description matches a Port Hand lateral mark?
bank.explanation: When entering a harbour with the flood tide, Port hand marks are red with square topmarks and should be left on the port (left) side.
options: Red with a square topmark, to be left on the port (left) side
Green with a conical topmark, to be left on the starboard (right) side
Red and white vertically striped with a spherical topmark
Yellow with an 'X' shape topmark

bank.question: What are the identifying colours of a 'Safe Water Mark'?
bank.explanation: Safe Water marks have vertical red and white stripes and a single red ball topmark
options: Horizontal red and black stripes
Yellow and black stripes
Vertical red and white stripes
Solid green with a cone topmark

bank.question: What are the physical characteristics of a 'Safe Water Mark'?
bank.explanation: A 'Safe Water Mark' has red and white vertical stripes and is often used to mark the transition from open water to a channel
options: Red and white vertical stripes with a single red ball topmark
Yellow and black horizontal stripes with two cones pointing up
Green and white horizontal stripes with a triangular topmark
Red and black horizontal stripes with two black spheres

bank.question: If your Magnetic bearing to a lighthouse is 090 degreesM and the Variation is 5 degreesE, what is the True bearing?
bank.explanation: Variation is East, so we subtract it from the Magnetic bearing to get the True bearing (Error East, Magnetic Least)
options: 095 DegreesT
085 DegreesT
090 DegreesT
100 DegreesT

bank.question: You are navigating near a rock and the chart indicates to pass to the East of the hazard. Which description identifies an East Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: An East Cardinal mark has two cones pointing away from each other (bases together) and indicates safe water to the East.
options: Two cones pointing away from each other (bases together)
Two cones pointing upwards
Two cones pointing downwards
Two cones pointing towards each other (points together)

bank.question: In coastal navigation, what is a 'Transit' (or Range)?
bank.explanation: Transits are highly accurate because they do not rely on a compass and visually confirm the vessel is on a specific line
options: A bearing taken using a hand-bearing compass
Two fixed objects seen in line with each other
A single distance measurement from a radar
The intersection of two GPS waypoints

bank.question: What does the 'Beaufort Scale' measure?
bank.explanation: The Beaufort Scale measures wind speed based on observable sea conditions or land effects, ranging from 0 (Calm) to 12 (Hurricane)
options: The rate of change in barometric pressure over 3 hours
The height of the waves in metres
A scale used to describe wind speed based on sea state or land conditions
The distance at which a light can be seen at night

bank.question: According to COLREGs, what does a black cylinder day shape indicate?
bank.explanation: A cylinder indicates a power-driven vessel constrained by its draught, meaning it is restricted in its ability to deviate from its course
options: A vessel at anchor
A vessel engaged in fishing
A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
A vessel constrained by her draught

bank.question: In a Course to Steer (CTS) diagram, which vector represents the Ground Track (the intended path over the seabed)?
bank.explanation: In a Course to Steer (CTS) diagram, the line with two arrows represents the 'Course Over Ground' (COG) or Ground Track.
options: The line with two arrows
The line representing the boat's heading
The line indicating the effect of current
The line showing the effect of leeway

bank.question: On a synoptic weather chart, what do closely spaced isobars generally indicate?
bank.explanation: Isobar spacing indicates the pressure gradient; closely packed lines mean the pressure changes rapidly over distance, resulting in stronger winds
options: Strong winds and steep pressure gradients
Light winds and stable weather
High humidity and heavy precipitation
Fog and poor visibility

bank.question: What is the topmark configuration for a West Cardinal Mark?
bank.explanation: A West Cardinal Mark has a yellow band in the middle of two black bands, and the cones point towards each other (waist to waist)
options: Cones pointing away from each other (base to base)
Cones pointing towards each other (point to point)
Two cones pointing upwards
Two cones pointing downwards

bank.question: When do 'Spring Tides' typically occur?
bank.explanation: Spring tides occur when the gravitational pull of the Sun and Moon are aligned, creating the greatest tidal range
options: Two days after a quarter moon
When the moon is at its furthest point from Earth
Shortly after a New or Full Moon
Only during the Equinoxes in March and September

bank.question: You observe a vessel at night. Which masthead light configuration signifies a 'Sailing Vessel' under way?
bank.explanation: A sailing vessel seen from the side at night shows a red (port) or green (starboard) sidelight; if over 20m or using optional lights, it may show red over green at the masthead.
options: Red over green at the masthead (if over 20m or using optional lights)
Three all-round white lights in a vertical line
Three all-round red lights in a vertical line
A single white masthead light with side lights

bank.question: In a crossing situation, what is the primary duty of the 'Give-way' vessel?
bank.explanation: The 'Give-way' vessel must take early and substantial action to remain well clear of the other vessel
options: Take early and substantial action to keep well clear
Maintain course and speed until the last moment
Turn to port to cross ahead of the other vessel
Stop the engines and wait for the other vessel to pass

bank.question: When two power-driven vessels are meeting on reciprocal courses head-on, what action should they take?
bank.explanation: COLREGs Rule 14 states that when two power-driven vessels are meeting head-on, both should alter course to starboard to pass on each other's port side
options: Both vessels should stop and wait for a signal
Both vessels should alter course to port
The smaller vessel must give way to the larger vessel
Both vessels should alter course to starboard

bank.question: What is the topmark and light characteristic of an East Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: An East Cardinal mark has two cones with bases together (diamond shape) and flashes in groups of 3 to match a clock face
options: Two cones pointing up; White light flashing continuously
Two cones pointing down; White light flashing in groups of 9
Two cones bases together; White light flashing in groups of 3
Two cones points together; White light flashing in groups of 6

bank.question: Which channel button should you select to monitor the international distress frequency?
bank.explanation: Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency used to establish initial contact before switching to a working channel.
options: Channel 16
Channel 68
Channel 70
Channel 72

bank.question: In a set of Admiralty Tide Tables, what is a 'Standard Port'?
bank.explanation: Standard Ports are places for which daily tide times and heights are specifically calculated and published in tide tables
options: Ports that allow vessels over 50 metres
A port where tidal predictions are based on daily observations
A port used only for refueling and customs
A port that uses the tides of another nearby location

bank.question: What are the characteristics of a 'Port Lateral Mark' in IALA Region A?
bank.explanation: In IALA Region A (which includes the UK), Port lateral marks are red with a can-shaped topmark
options: Red colour and a can-shaped topmark
Green colour and a cone-shaped topmark
Red colour and a cone-shaped topmark
Green colour and a can-shaped topmark

bank.question: What is the definition of 'Chart Datum'?
bank.explanation: Chart Datum is the plane below which the tide rarely falls, providing a conservative height for safety
options: The highest astronomical tide recorded
The mean level between high and low water
The average depth of the sea over 100 years
A level below which the tide will seldom fall

bank.question: You are approaching a cluster of rocks and must pass to the West of the hazard. Which description identifies a West Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: A West Cardinal mark has two cones point-to-point (forming a 'waist' shape) and indicates safe water is to the West of the mark.
options: Two cones point-to-point (forming a 'waist' shape)
Two cones pointing upwards
Two cones pointing downwards
Two cones pointing away from each other (bases together)

bank.question: What lights must a vessel 'Not Under Command' show at night when making way?
bank.explanation: A vessel 'not under command' is unable to manoeuvre as required by the rules due to some exceptional circumstance, like engine failure
options: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line
Two all-round white lights in a vertical line
A red light over a white light
Three all-round red lights in a vertical line

bank.question: What is 'Leeway' in the context of boat handling and navigation?
bank.explanation: Leeway is the leeward (downwind) drift of a vessel caused by the wind blowing against the hull and rigging
options: The error caused by magnetic interference on a compass
The distance traveled over the ground in one hour
The sideways drift of a vessel caused by the wind
The difference between magnetic north and true north

bank.question: If MHWS is 5.2m and MLWS is 0.8m, what is the 'Spring Range'?
bank.explanation: Spring range is the difference between Mean High Water Springs and Mean Low Water Springs. 5.2m - 0.8m = 4.4m
options: 5.2 Metres
6.0 Metres
4.4 Metres
0.8 Metres

bank.question: When planning a passage and using a vector triangle, which vector represents the Course to Steer (heading through the water)?
bank.explanation: In a Course to Steer (CTS) triangle, the vector with one arrow represents the path through the water (vessel's heading and speed).
options: The vector showing leeway
The vector with a single arrow indicating the vessel's heading and speed
The vector representing the true course over the ground
The vector indicating tidal set and drift

bank.question: When describing wind direction changes, what does the term 'Veering' mean?
bank.explanation: Veering refers to the wind shifting in a clockwise direction (e.g., North to North-East). Moving anti-clockwise is called backing
options: Changing direction anti-clockwise
Changing direction clockwise
Increasing in strength suddenly
Decreasing in strength suddenly

bank.question: From which reference level are charted depths measured?
bank.explanation: Depths on UK Hydrographic Office charts are measured from 'Chart Datum', which is typically the Lowest Astronomical Tide (LAT)
options: The highest astronomical tide level
The Lowest Astronomical Tide (LAT)
The mean sea level over a 19-year period
The depth at the time the survey ship passed over

bank.question: What is the topmark of a South Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: A South Cardinal mark is yellow on top and black on bottom, with two cones pointing downwards as its topmark
options: Two black cones pointing upwards
Two black cones pointing downwards
Two black cones pointing towards each other
Two black cones pointing away from each other

bank.question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, where Vessel A has Vessel B on her starboard side, which vessel is the give-way vessel?
bank.explanation: Rule 15 states that when two power-driven vessels are crossing, the vessel which has the other on her own starboard side shall keep out of the way. Therefore, Vessel A is the give-way vessel as Vessel B is on her starboard side.
options: Vessel B
Both vessels are give-way vessels
Vessel A
Neither vessel is a give-way vessel

bank.question: Which of the following describes a 'backstay' on a sailing vessel?
bank.explanation: A 'backstay' is part of the standing rigging that runs from the top of the mast to the stern to prevent the mast from falling forward
options: The wire running from the mast to the bow
The rope used to pull the mainsail up the mast
The ropes used to trim the jib or genoa
A wire or rope supporting the mast from the stern

bank.question: According to COLREGs, what is a vessel 'Not Under Command'?
bank.explanation: A vessel 'not under command' (NUC) is one that, through some exceptional circumstance, is unable to manoeuvre as required by the rules
options: A vessel that is at anchor in a busy channel
A vessel that has run out of fuel
A vessel engaged in fishing with nets
A vessel which through some exceptional circumstance is unable to manoeuvre

bank.question: In a maneuvering situation, what does one short blast on the whistle mean?
bank.explanation: A single short blast (approx. 1 second) indicates that a vessel is altering her course to starboard
options: I am altering my course to starboard
I am altering my course to port
I am operating astern propulsion
I am unsure of your intentions

bank.question: You are approaching a shallow bank and must pass to the south of it. Which cardinal mark indicates the safe water lies to the south?
bank.explanation: A South Cardinal mark features two cones pointing downwards and a yellow-over-black colour scheme, indicating safe water to the south.
options: A West Cardinal mark
An East Cardinal mark
A North Cardinal mark
A South Cardinal mark

bank.question: What does the term 'Ground Track' (or Course Made Good) represent in navigation?
bank.explanation: A 'Ground Track' is the actual path of the vessel over the seabed, accounting for both tide and leeway
options: The direction the boat's bow is pointing
The path of the boat through the water only
The actual path of the vessel over the seabed
The distance calculated by the log

bank.question: In tidal terminology, what does 'Duration' refer to?
bank.explanation: The 'Duration' of a tide is the length of time between a high water and the subsequent low water (or vice versa)
options: The time elapsed between high water and low water
The distance between high water and low water heights
The speed at which the tidal stream is flowing
The period during which the tide is completely slack

bank.question: What night-time lights must a vessel 'Constrained by her Draught' display in addition to her standard running lights?
bank.explanation: A vessel 'Constrained by her Draught' displays three all-round red lights in a vertical line at night
options: Three all-round green lights in a vertical line
Three all-round red lights in a vertical line
A red light over a white light
Two all-round red lights in a vertical line

bank.question: When plotting an Estimated Position (EP) based on a DR line, which vector represents the 'Tide' (Set and Drift)?
bank.explanation: When plotting an Estimated Position (EP), the tidal vector is drawn from the DR position in the direction the tide is setting.
options: The vector showing the vessel's course over ground
The vector drawn from the DR position in the direction the tide is setting
The vector representing the vessel's speed through the water
The vector indicating leeway caused by wind

bank.question: In weather terminology, what does it mean when the wind is 'Backing'?
bank.explanation: When 'Backing', the wind direction changes in an anti-clockwise direction (e.g., North to North-West)
options: The wind is increasing in speed
The wind is decreasing in speed
The wind direction is changing clockwise
The wind direction is changing anti-clockwise

bank.question: According to COLREG Rule 9, where should a vessel navigate in a narrow channel?
bank.explanation: In a 'Narrow Channel' (Rule 9), vessels should keep as near to the outer limit of the channel which lies on their starboard side as is safe and practicable
options: Steer in the middle of the channel to avoid shallows
Keep to the port side to allow faster vessels to pass
Keep as near to the outer limit on the starboard side as is safe
Always give way to sailing vessels regardless of side

bank.question: Under the IALA Region A buoyage system, what is the colour scheme for a 'Preferred Channel to Starboard' mark?
bank.explanation: At the entrance to a channel, a Preferred Channel to Starboard mark is red with one horizontal green band
options: Red with one horizontal green band
Green with one horizontal red band
Red and white vertical stripes
Yellow and black horizontal bands

bank.question: Which lighting configuration at night indicates a vessel that is 'Constrained by her Draught' and unable to deviate from her course?
bank.explanation: A vessel constrained by her draught displays three red all-round lights in a vertical line at night.
options: Two green all-round lights in a vertical line
Three red all-round lights in a vertical line
A single flashing yellow light
Three white masthead lights in a vertical line

bank.question: If your True course is 045 degreesT and the Variation is 7 degreesW, what is your Magnetic course?
bank.explanation: Using the mnemonic 'Variation West, Magnetic Best', you add westerly variation to a True bearing to find the Magnetic bearing (045 + 7 = 052)
options: 038 DegreesM
052 DegreesM
045 DegreesM
060 DegreesM

bank.question: What does a rapidly falling barometric pressure usually indicate?
bank.explanation: The 'Sinking' or 'Falling' of the barometer usually precedes the arrival of a depression (low pressure), which often brings wind and rain
options: Wind and rain are likely approaching
Dry, settled, and sunny weather is expected
The wind is about to die down completely
Fog is guaranteed to form within the hour

bank.question: What are the identifying colours of an 'Isolated Danger Mark'?
bank.explanation: An isolated danger mark is placed directly over a hazard and is black with one or more horizontal red bands
options: Yellow and black horizontal stripes
Red and white vertical stripes
Black with one or more horizontal red bands
Solid green with a cone topmark

bank.question: When moored alongside a pontoon in a cross-wind, which line is described as a 'Stern Breast' used to keep the aft of the boat tight against the pontoon?
bank.explanation: The breast back is a short line led roughly at 90 degrees to the pontoon to hold the stern in close.
options: A bow spring line
A line led from the bow to the shore
A short line led roughly at 90 degrees to the pontoon to hold the stern in close
An aft spring line

bank.question: When do 'Neap Tides' typically occur?
bank.explanation: Neap tides occur when the moon is at its first or last quarter, resulting in the smallest tidal range
options: During a Full Moon
During a New Moon
During the first and last quarter of the moon phase
When the sun and moon are in direct alignment

bank.question: What are the colours and light characteristics of a North Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: A North Cardinal mark is black over yellow, and its light flashes continuously (either Quick or Very Quick)
options: Yellow with a black band in the middle, flashing Q(6)+LFl 15s
Black with a yellow band in the middle, flashing Fl(3) 10s
Black at the top and yellow at the bottom, flashing Q or VQ continuous
Yellow at the top and black at the bottom, flashing Q(9) 15s

bank.question: What are the identification lights for a vessel engaged in fishing, other than trawling?
bank.explanation: A vessel engaged in fishing (other than trawling) displays a red light over a white light. (Note: Trawling is green over white)
options: Green light over a white light
Red light over a white light
White light over a red light
Two red lights in a vertical line

bank.question: Which knot is most suitable for securing a vessel to a metal ring on a harbour wall, as it's least likely to jam under tension and is easy to untie?
bank.explanation: The Round Turn and Two Half Hitches is the most reliable knot for securing a boat to a ring or post under load as it won't jam and is easy to untie.
options: A Reef Knot
A Bowline
A Clove hitch
The Round Turn and Two Half Hitches

bank.question: Under COLREGs Rule 14, how should two power-driven vessels act when meeting on nearly reciprocal courses?
bank.explanation: Rule 14 states that when two power-driven vessels are meeting on reciprocal courses, both shall alter course to starboard to pass on the port side of each other
options: Maintain course and speed; the larger vessel has right of way
Alter course to port to pass on the starboard side of the other vessel
Alter course to starboard to pass on the port side of the other vessel
Stop engines and wait for the other vessel to pass

bank.question: Entering a harbour in IALA Region A, you see a pillar buoy with 'Red-Green-Red' horizontal bands. What does this indicate?
bank.explanation: In IALA Region A, a Preferred Channel to Starboard mark is red with one horizontal green band
options: Red with one horizontal green band
Green with one horizontal red band
Red and white vertical stripes
Yellow and black horizontal stripes

bank.question: In coastal navigation, what does the term 'Leeway' specifically refer to?
bank.explanation: Leeway is the leeward motion of a vessel caused by the wind pushing the hull and rigging, requiring an adjustment to the steered course to maintain the intended track
options: The speed of the vessel through the water
The sideways drift of a vessel caused by the wind
The effect of the tide on a vessel's speed over ground
The difference between Magnetic North and True North

bank.question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, according to ColRegs Rule 15, which vessel is the 'Stand-on' vessel?
bank.explanation: Under IRPCS Rule 15, when two power-driven vessels are crossing, the vessel which has the other on her own starboard side shall keep out of the way. Therefore, the vessel that does NOT have the other on her starboard side (i.e., has the other on her port side) is the stand-on vessel.
options: The vessel which has the other on her own port side
The vessel which has the other on her own starboard side
The vessel travelling at a higher speed
The vessel that sounds a warning signal first

bank.question: What is the colour sequence (from top to bottom) for a West Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: A West Cardinal mark has a black band in the middle with yellow bands at the top and bottom, and its cones point inward (point-to-point)
options: Yellow with a single broad horizontal black band in the middle
Black with a single broad horizontal yellow band in the middle
Yellow at the top and black at the bottom
Black at the top and yellow at the bottom

bank.question: What is the topmark for a South Cardinal buoy?
bank.explanation: A South Cardinal mark has two cones pointing downwards, reflecting the black band at the bottom of the buoy
options: Cones pointing away from each other (base to base)
Cones pointing downwards
Cones pointing towards each other (point to point)
Cones pointing upwards

bank.question: When do 'Spring Tides' occur in the lunar cycle?
bank.explanation: Spring tides occur when the gravitational pull of the Sun and Moon are aligned (at New and Full moon), creating the greatest tidal range
options: When the moon is at its first quarter
Only during the summer months in the UK
When the moon is at its third quarter
Near the times of New Moon and Full Moon

bank.question: You are navigating near a submerged wreck and the chart indicates you must pass to the North for safe water. Which Cardinal Mark would you look for?
bank.explanation: A North Cardinal mark indicates that the deepest or safest water lies to the North; its topmark consists of two cones pointing upwards.
options: An East Cardinal mark
A West Cardinal mark
A North Cardinal mark
A South Cardinal mark

bank.question: What is the topmark for a 'Safe Water Mark' (e.g., Fairway Buoy)?
bank.explanation: A Safe Water Mark, often used as a landfall or fairway buoy, displays a single red ball as its topmark
options: A single red sphere (ball)
Two black spheres (balls) arranged vertically
A red upright cross
A yellow 'X' shape

bank.question: When do Spring Tides typically occur?
bank.explanation: Spring tides occur when the Sun and Moon are aligned, creating the greatest gravitational pull and highest tidal range
options: When the moon is in its first or third quarter
During a solar eclipse only
When the wind blows from the south for three days
Near the time of a New or Full moon

bank.question: Which of the following is a recognised distress signal under COLREGs Annex IV?
bank.explanation: A continuous sounding of any fog-signalling apparatus is one of several internationally recognised distress signals listed in Annex IV of COLREGs
options: One short blast every 2 minutes
A continuous sounding with any fog-signalling apparatus
Three short blasts followed by three long blasts
A single green flare fired at five-minute intervals

bank.question: Which light characteristic describes an 'Occulting' light, such as a lighthouse with the characteristic 'Oc 10s'?
bank.explanation: An occulting light is one where the total duration of light in each period is longer than the total duration of darkness.
options: A light where the total duration of darkness is longer than the total duration of light in each period
A light that flashes at irregular intervals
A light that shows a single continuous light for 10 seconds
A light where the total duration of light in each period is longer than the total duration of darkness

bank.question: In pilotage, what is the 'Squat' effect?
bank.explanation: The 'Squat' effect occurs when a vessel moving through shallow water creates a pressure drop that causes the hull to sink deeper into the water
options: The vessel's tendency to turn into the wind
Excessive rolling caused by Following Seas
The increase in speed due to following tide
The reduction in under-keel clearance because of a vessel's speed through the water

bank.question: What lights must a sailing vessel under 20 metres exhibit while underway at night?
bank.explanation: Standard COLREGs require a sailing vessel under 20m to show sidelights and a sternlight when under sail alone
options: A single all-round white light
A red light over a green light at the masthead
Red and Green sidelights and a white sternlight
A steaming light and sidelights

bank.question: In a narrow channel, which side is a vessel required to keep to?
bank.explanation: When navigating in a narrow channel, Rule 9 requires all vessels to stay as near to the outer limit of the channel on their starboard side as is safe and practicable
options: Stay in the deepest part of the channel regardless of side
Stay to the port side of the channel
Stay as near to the outer limit of the channel on the starboard side as is safe
Keep to the centre of the channel to allow others to pass on either side

bank.question: Which type of line prevents a boat from moving forward when moored alongside a pontoon, especially with a strong tide pushing it ahead?
bank.explanation: The aft spring prevents the vessel from moving forward while moored alongside.
options: Aft spring line
Forward breast line
Bow line
Stern line

bank.question: In meteorology, what defines a 'Cold Front'?
bank.explanation: A 'Cold Front' occurs when a mass of colder, denser air pushes under a mass of warmer air, often resulting in heavy rain and a sudden wind shift
options: Cold air moving in and replacing warmer air
Warm air moving in and replacing colder air
A front that has stopped moving entirely
The point where a cold front overtakes a warm front

bank.question: To convert tidal times from UT (GMT) to British Summer Time (BST), what action must you take?
bank.explanation: Standard Time (UT/GMT) is used in nearly all nautical tables; you must add one hour to calculate BST
options: Subtract 1 hour from the table time
Add 1 hour to the table time
No change is needed as tides follow UTC
Add 2 hours to the table time

bank.question: What type of weather front is formed when a cold front catches up with a warm front?
bank.explanation: An 'Occluded Front' forms when a fast-moving cold front overtakes a warm front, lifting the warm air entirely off the ground
options: A Stationary Front
An Occluded Front
A High Pressure Ridge
A Squall Line

bank.question: When navigating in open water, which buoy topmark indicates an 'Isolated Danger' marking a specific, small hazard such as a submerged rock or wreck?
bank.explanation: The Isolated Danger mark is placed directly over a hazard of limited extent and is identified by two black spheres.
options: Two black spheres
Two red cones, points together
A single black can
A yellow 'X' shape

bank.question: What are the vertical identification lights for a vessel 'Engaged in Trawling' at night?
bank.explanation: Rule 26 states that a vessel engaged in trawling must show a green light over a white light in a vertical line. Think 'Green over White, Trawling at night'
options: Red over White
Red over Red
Green over White
White over Red

bank.question: What is the day signal/lights for a vessel Restricted in her Ability to Manoeuvre (RAM)?
bank.explanation: A vessel 'Restricted in her Ability to Manoeuvre' (such as a dredger or cable layer) shows Red-White-Red vertical lights
options: Three all-round lights in a vertical line: Red-White-Red
Two all-round red lights in a vertical line
Three all-round red lights in a vertical line
One all-round green light over one all-round white light

bank.question: Which part of a boat is referred to as the 'Transom'?
bank.explanation: The Transom refers to the flat surface forming the stern (the back) of a boat
options: The front of the boat (the bow)
The lower part of the keel
The flat surface forming the stern of the boat
The horizontal spar used to extend the foot of a sail

bank.question: When allowing for the wind's effect on a vessel's heading, which vector represents the boat's path through the water AFTER leeway has been applied?
bank.explanation: Leeway is applied 'downwind' from the Water Track to find the Course Made Good through the water.
options: Course Made Good
Water Track
Ground Track
Heading

bank.question: On a UK nautical chart, what does the 'Charted Depth' (sounding) represent?
bank.explanation: The depth shown on the chart is the depth at Chart Datum; the height of the tide must be added to determine the actual depth at that time
options: The shallowest possible water at that location
The depth of water during a Spring tide
The depth of water at the lowest astronomical tide (LAT)
The depth of water exactly at high tide

bank.question: What weather changes are typically associated with the passage of a Cold Front?
bank.explanation: Squalls and heavy rain are characteristic of a cold front as it pushes under warm air, creating unstable conditions
options: Lowering clouds and steady light drizzle
Clear skies and light winds from the East
A sudden veer in wind direction, a drop in temperature, and heavy rain/squalls
Falling pressure with rising temperatures and fog

bank.question: What does a day shape consisting of two black balls in a vertical line indicate?
bank.explanation: Two black balls in a vertical line signify a vessel that through some exceptional circumstance is unable to manoeuvre as required by the rules
options: A vessel Not Under Command (NUC)
A vessel Aground
A vessel engaged in Underwater Operations
A vessel Constrained by her Draught

bank.question: At night, a vessel displaying two all-round lights in a vertical line, the top one red and the lower one white, indicates which type of vessel?
bank.explanation: The 'Red over White' lights indicate a vessel engaged in fishing other than trawling.
options: A fishing vessel (other than trawling)
A vessel at anchor
A power-driven vessel underway
A vessel restricted in its ability to manoeuvre

bank.question: In navigation, what is the definition of 'Magnetic Variation'?
bank.explanation: Variation is the angular difference between Magnetic North and True North, which changes depending on your location on Earth and the year
options: The error caused by magnetic items on the boat
The angle between True North and Magnetic North
The movement of the boat due to the wind
The difference between the compass heading and the waypoint

bank.question: In tidal calculations, what is a 'Standard Port'?
bank.explanation: The 'Standard Port' is the primary port for which full daily predictions are provided in the tide tables
options: The port where the vessel is currently berthed
A port for which daily time and height predictions are provided in the tables
Any port that has a harbour master's office
A port that uses a different time zone than the local area

bank.question: What is the topmark for a North Cardinal buoy?
bank.explanation: A North Cardinal mark is black on top and yellow on the bottom; both cones point upwards, indicating the safe water is to the North
options: Two cones pointing towards each other
Two cones pointing away from each other
Two cones pointing downwards
Two cones pointing upwards

bank.question: Under COLREGs, if a power-driven vessel (Vessel B) and a sailing vessel (Vessel A) are in sight of one another, which vessel is required to give way?
bank.explanation: Under COLREGs Rule 18, a power-driven vessel must keep out of the way of a sailing vessel. Vessel B is the power-driven give-way vessel.
options: Vessel B (power-driven)
Vessel A (sailing)
Neither, they both must alter course
The vessel on the starboard side

bank.question: Under COLREGs, if a sailing vessel (using sails only) is overtaking a power-driven vessel from behind, which vessel must give way?
bank.explanation: According to COLREG Rule 13, any vessel overtaking another must keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken
options: The sailing vessel is stand-on because it is under sail
Both vessels must alter course to starboard
The power-driven vessel is the give-way vessel
The sailing vessel is the give-way vessel

bank.question: How is the height of tide calculated for a 'Secondary Port'?
bank.explanation: Secondary ports use time and height differences applied to a nearby Standard Port's data
options: Applying time and height differences to a Standard Port
Multiplying the Standard Port height by two
Subtracting the charted depth from the Lowest Astronomical Tide
Consulting a different set of tables that only cover Secondary Ports

bank.question: What is the recommended minimum length of anchor chain to deploy in normal conditions for an overnight stay?
bank.explanation: The RYA suggest 4 times the depth for chain and 6 times the depth for a rope/chain warp for a standard overnight stay
options: 4 Times the depth of water
2 Times the depth of water
10 Times the depth of water
Exactly the depth of water plus the freeboard

bank.question: When entering a port where the channel divides, which buoy indicates a 'Preferred Channel to Starboard'?
bank.explanation: A Preferred Channel to Starboard mark is a red lateral buoy with one horizontal green band. It is used when a channel divides.
options: A red lateral buoy with one horizontal green band
A green lateral buoy with one horizontal red band
A red and white vertically striped buoy
A yellow cardinal buoy

bank.question: When must a vessel maintain a proper look-out according to COLREG Rule 5?
bank.explanation: Rule 5 states that every vessel shall at all times maintain a proper look-out by sight and hearing as well as by all available means
options: Only when visibility is restricted (e.g. fog)
Only when the vessel is moving at over 5 knots
Only when navigating in busy shipping lanes
At all times, including at anchor and regardless of visibility

bank.question: According to COLREGs, what is the definition of a vessel 'Constrained by her Draught'?
bank.explanation: A vessel 'Constrained by her Draught' is a power-driven vessel that has limited room to manoeuvre due to its depth relative to the water
options: A vessel fishing with nets or trawls
A sailing vessel in a narrow channel
A vessel unable to move due to engine failure
A power-driven vessel which, because of her draught, is severely restricted in her ability to deviate from her course

bank.question: In a shipping forecast, what does it mean if the wind is 'Veering'?
bank.explanation: A 'Veering' wind shifts in a clockwise direction (e.g., South-West to West). A 'Backing' wind shifts anti-clockwise
options: The wind is increasing in speed
The wind is shifting in a clockwise direction
The wind is shifting in an anti-clockwise direction
The wind is decreasing in speed/strength

bank.question: When plotting an Estimated Position (EP), which vector represents the tidal 'Set and Drift'?
bank.explanation: In an Estimated Position (EP) plot, the 'Set and Drift' vector represents the direction and distance the tide has moved the vessel during the period.
options: The vector showing the direction and distance the tide has moved the vessel
The vector showing the boat's speed through the water
The vector showing the vessel's intended course
The vector showing the effect of wind on the vessel

bank.question: What is the appearance of a 'Special Mark' in IALA Region A?
bank.explanation: Special marks are used to indicate specific features like outfalls or race marks; they are yellow and have an 'X' topmark
options: A red and white striped buoy
A yellow buoy with an 'X' topmark
A green buoy with a cone topmark
A black and yellow buoy with two cones

bank.question: What are the primary radio frequencies used by a modern EPIRB to alert search and rescue authorities?
bank.explanation: Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacons (EPIRBs) transmit on 406 MHz to satellites and often 121.5 MHz for local homing
options: VHF Channel 16 and 70
406 MHz and 121.5 MHz
2.4 GHz and 5 GHz
MF 2182 kHz only

bank.question: What two main pieces of information are used to plot a 'Dead Reckoning' (DR) position?
bank.explanation: Dead Reckoning (DR) uses the course steered and the distance through the water (log) only, ignoring external forces like tide
options: Course Steered and Distance through the water (Log) only
Course Steered, Log Speed, and Leeway
Course Over Ground and Tide Speed
Course Steered, Log Speed, Tide, and Leeway

bank.question: Which knot, forming a fixed loop, is most reliable for attaching a halyard to the head of a sail?
bank.explanation: A bowline creates a secure, non-slipping loop at the end of a line, making it the most reliable knot for securing a halyard to a sail.
options: Bowline
Figure-of-eight knot
Reef knot
Clove hitch

bank.question: In open water, which vessel is the give-way vessel when a power-driven vessel meets a vessel 'Restricted in her Ability to Manoeuvre'?
bank.explanation: Rule 18 sets the hierarchy: a power-driven vessel must give way to a vessel restricted in its ability to manoeuvre
options: The vessel Restricted in her Ability to Manoeuvre (RAM)
Neither, they should both stop immediately
The vessel that has the other on its port side
The power-driven vessel

bank.question: What does a spherical buoy with red and white vertical stripes indicate?
bank.explanation: A Safe Water Mark is used to indicate that there is navigable water all around the position
options: Navigable water all around the mark
The entrance to a narrow channel
The deepest part of a shipwreck
A speed restriction zone

bank.question: In a UK Sea State forecast, what is the approximate wave height range for a 'Very High' sea?
