bank.explanation: A 'very high' Sea State in the Douglas Scale or similar forecast terms refers to waves between 9 and 14 metres in height
options: 0 - 0.5 Metres
1 - 2 Metres
9 - 14 Metres
Over 20 metres

bank.question: What is the correct topmark for an 'Isolated Danger' buoy, indicating a small hazard with navigable water all around it?
bank.explanation: An Isolated Danger mark features two black spheres as its topmark and indicates a hazard with navigable water all around it.
options: Two black spheres
A single red sphere
Two black cones, points up
A single black column

bank.question: What are the topmarks and colour sequence for a South Cardinal buoy?
bank.explanation: A South Cardinal mark features two downward-pointing cones and a yellow-over-black colour scheme
options: Two cones pointing towards each other; Black with a yellow band in the middle
Two cones pointing upwards; Black over yellow
Two cones pointing downwards; Yellow over black
Two cones pointing away from each other; Yellow with a black band in the middle

bank.question: What is the colour and arc of visibility for a stern light?
bank.explanation: The transom/stern light for a power-driven vessel must be a white light showing over an arc of 135 degrees
options: White, 360 degrees
Yellow, 112.5 degrees
White, 135 degrees
Red, 225 degrees

bank.question: What is the minimum requirement for navigation lights for a 10-metre power-driven vessel making way at night?
bank.explanation: Under COLREGs, power-driven vessels under 12m may exhibit an all-round white light and sidelights
options: A single all-round white light only
An all-round white light and sidelights
A masthead light, stern light, and sidelights
Two all-round red lights

bank.question: Which day shape indicates a vessel that is 'Restricted in her Ability to Manoeuvre'?
bank.explanation: A vessel engaged in a towing operation that is unable to deviate from its course is 'Restricted in her Ability to Manoeuvre' and shows the Ball-Diamond-Ball day shape.
options: Ball-Diamond-Ball
Cylinder
Cone, point down
Two balls in a vertical line

bank.question: In navigation, what is meant by the term 'Leeway'?
bank.explanation: Leeway is the downwind movement of a vessel caused by the wind pushing against the hull and superstructure
options: The distance a vessel is pushed sideways off its course by the wind
The effect of a tidal stream on a vessel's track
The vertical distance between the keel and the seabed
The difference between Magnetic North and True North

bank.question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel is the 'give-way' vessel?
bank.explanation: Rule 14 states that when two power-driven vessels are crossing so as to involve risk of collision, the vessel which has the other on her own starboard side shall keep out of the way
options: The vessel to port stays clear
The vessel that has the other on her own starboard side stays clear
The faster vessel stays clear
The vessel with the wind on her port side stays clear

bank.question: What is the 'Range' of a tide?
bank.explanation: The spring range is the difference between Mean High Water Springs and Mean Low Water Springs
options: The time elapsed between high tide and the following low tide
The distance a vessel travels during a six-hour tidal cycle
The depth of water available at a specific location at high tide
The vertical difference in height between high water and low water during a spring tide

bank.question: Which vector represents the 'Ground Track' (Course Over Ground) after you have plotted your Course to Steer and applied the tide?
bank.explanation: The Course Over Ground (COG) or 'Ground Track' is represented by the vector with two arrows, showing the boat's actual path relative to the seabed.
options: A vector showing a single arrow, indicating the intended heading relative to the water.
A vector showing two arrows, indicating the vessel's actual path relative to the seabed.
A vector indicating the direction and speed of the tidal stream.
A vector indicating the direction and speed of the wind.

bank.question: In the RYA tidal tables, what defines a 'Secondary Port'?
bank.explanation: Secondary ports are calculated using a 'Standard Port' as a reference, applying time and height differences
options: A port that only allows entry during daylight hours
A port for which tidal predictions are calculated by applying differences to a 'Standard Port'
A port used only when the primary destination is inaccessible due to weather
A port situated on a river rather than the open coast

bank.question: In compass navigation, what is 'Deviation'?
bank.explanation: Deviation is the error caused by local magnetic fields on the vessel, such as the engine, electronics, or metal equipment
options: The angle between Magnetic North and True North
The movement of the boat caused by the wind
The error caused by the Earth's shifting poles
The error caused by magnetic influences on board the vessel

bank.question: According to COLREGs, if two power-driven vessels are meeting on reciprocal (head-on) courses, what action should they take?
bank.explanation: Under Rule 14, when two power-driven vessels meet head-on, both must alter course to starboard to pass on each other's port side
options: Both vessels should stop and wait for the other to signal
Both vessels should alter course to port
Both vessels should alter course to starboard
The smaller vessel must give way to the larger vessel

bank.question: When identifying a cardinal mark at night, which light characteristic identifies an East Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: An East Cardinal mark flashes in groups of 3 (representing 3 o'clock on a clock face) to assist with quick identification.
options: Continuous quick or very quick flashes.
Groups of 9 quick or very quick flashes.
Groups of 3 quick or very quick flashes.
Groups of 6 quick or very quick flashes followed by a long flash.

bank.question: What is the topmark for a 'Port Hand' lateral buoy in IALA Region A?
bank.explanation: A Cylinder topmark is used exclusively for Port Hand marks in IALA Region A
options: Cylinder (Can)
Cone (Triangle)
Sphere (Ball)
Two balls in a vertical line

bank.question: What term describes the period of minimum tidal range?
bank.explanation: The 'Neap' range is the smallest difference between high and low water, occurring when the moon is in its first or third quarter
options: Neap range
Spring range
Mean Sea Level
Tidal surge

bank.question: On a synoptic weather chart, what do 'Isobars' represent?
bank.explanation: Isobars connect points of equal atmospheric pressure; closely spaced isobars signal a steep pressure gradient and high winds
options: Points of equal air temperature
Points of equal rainfall
Areas of clear sky
Points of equal atmospheric pressure

bank.question: You are in a narrow channel and hear a power-driven vessel sound two short blasts. What does this sound signal indicate?
bank.explanation: Under ColRegs, two short blasts indicate 'I am altering my course to port'.
options: I am altering my course to starboard.
I intend to overtake you on your starboard side.
I am altering my course to port.
I am operating astern propulsion.

bank.question: What is an 'Estimated Position' (EP) in navigation?
bank.explanation: A 'Estimated Position' (EP) includes the vessel's movement through the water (DR) plus the effects of tide and leeway
options: A position fixed by three visual bearings
A position calculated by applying tide and leeway to a Dead Reckoning (DR) position
A position obtained solely from a GPS receiver
The position of a vessel at the start of a passage

bank.question: What are Isobars on a synoptic weather chart?
bank.explanation: Isobar lines on a weather map connect areas of equal atmospheric pressure. Lines close together indicate strong winds
options: Lines of equal temperature
Lines of equal atmospheric pressure
Lines of equal depth
Lines of equal rainfall

bank.question: When do 'Spring Tides' generally occur?
bank.explanation: Spring tides occur when the gravitational pull of the Sun and Moon are aligned (New or Full Moon), causing the greatest tidal range
options: When the Moon is at its first and last quarter
When the wind is blowing in the same direction as the tide
When the Moon, Sun, and Earth are in alignment (New or Full Moon)
When the atmospheric pressure is exceptionally high

bank.question: You are navigating near a sandbar and need to pass to the West of the hazard. How is a West Cardinal mark identified?
bank.explanation: A West Cardinal mark has cones pointing point-to-point (forming a wine glass or 'W' shape) and a yellow band between two black bands.
options: Cones pointing upward, black over yellow, with continuous quick flashes.
Cones pointing downward, yellow over black, with 9 quick flashes.
Cones pointing point-to-point (forming a 'W' shape), with a yellow band between two black bands, and 9 quick flashes.
Cones pointing base-to-base, black over yellow, with 3 quick flashes.

bank.question: What day shape must a vessel 'Aground' exhibit?
bank.explanation: Three black balls in a vertical line represent a vessel aground during daylight hours
options: Three black balls in a vertical line
A cylinder
Two black balls in a vertical line
A black diamond

bank.question: Which buoy is black with one or more horizontal red bands and has two black spheres as a topmark?
bank.explanation: An Isolated Danger mark is placed directly on or over an isolated hazard that has navigable water all around it
options: North Cardinal Mark
Special Mark
Isolated Danger Mark
Emergency Wreck Buoy

bank.question: Which VHF channel is designated for 'Distress, Safety and Calling'?
bank.explanation: Channel 16 is the international frequency for distress, safety, and calling, used to establish initial contact before switching
options: Channel 06
Channel 12
Channel 72
Channel 16

bank.question: When planning a passage across a tidal stream, which vector represents your Course to Steer (Water Track)?
bank.explanation: The Course to Steer (heading) vector is represented by a line with one arrow, used to counteract tide and leeway.
options: A vector showing two arrows, indicating the vessel's path relative to the seabed.
A vector showing a single arrow, indicating the intended heading relative to the water.
A vector representing the direction and speed of the tidal current.
A vector representing the direction and speed of the wind and waves.

bank.question: Under COLREGs, what day shape must a sailing vessel display when also being propelled by machinery?
bank.explanation: A sailing vessel under power (even if sails are up) is legally a power-driven vessel and must display a conical shape pointing downwards
options: A black ball
Two black diamonds in a vertical line
A cylinder (can) shape
A black cone, point downwards

bank.question: What is a 'Transit' in coastal navigation?
bank.explanation: A transit (or range) is a highly accurate position line formed when two fixed objects on land are seen to be vertically in line
options: The distance between two buoys
A fix using three different compass bearings
The time taken to travel between two points
A position line formed by two charted objects appearing in line

bank.question: What is the 'Rule of Twelfths' used for in UK tidal calculations?
bank.explanation: The Rule of Twelfths is a method for estimating the gradual increase and decrease in tidal height during each hour of the six-hour flood or ebb
options: A way to calculate the depth of the anchor chain
An estimate of how much the tide rises or falls in each of the six hours between high and low water
The rule for determining the speed of a tidal stream in knots
A formula for calculating the fuel consumption of a diesel engine

bank.question: At night, you see a vessel displaying three white masthead lights in a vertical line. What does this indicate?
bank.explanation: A vessel towing with a tow length exceeding 200m displays three vertical white masthead lights in addition to sidelights and a stern light.
options: A vessel at anchor.
A vessel pushing ahead or towing alongside.
A vessel towing another where the length of the tow exceeds 200 metres.
A vessel constrained by her draught.

bank.question: Under COLREGs, if two power-driven vessels are crossing so as to involve risk of collision, which one must give way?
bank.explanation: Rule 15 states that when two power-driven vessels are crossing, the vessel which has the other on her own starboard side shall keep out of the way
options: The vessel on the left (port) is the stand-on vessel
The larger vessel always has right of way
The vessel that has the other on her own starboard side must give way
Both vessels must turn to port immediately

bank.question: Which light is a sailing vessel NOT allowed to show if she is proceeding under sail alone?
bank.explanation: Rule 25 states that a sailing vessel under sail alone shall exhibit sidelights and a stern light. If under 20m, these may be combined in a tricolour
options: A steaming light (masthead light)
Red and Green sidelights + Stern light
A single all-round white light
Two all-round red lights in a vertical line

bank.question: What is 'Chart Datum'?
bank.explanation: Chart Datum is the level below which the tide rarely falls; depths on a chart are measured downwards from this reference level
options: The plane of reference for all depths shown on a nautical chart
The average height of the highest spring tides
The distance from the seabed to the waterline of the vessel
The height of the mast above the water level

bank.question: Which anchor is known for its good holding power in sandy seabeds?
bank.explanation: The CQR (or plough) anchor is a versatile, high-holding-power anchor that is excellent for use in sand and mud.
options: The Danforth anchor, designed for mud and sand.
The Grapnel anchor, primarily used for dinghies.
The CQR (or plough) anchor, excellent for sand and mud.
The Fisherman's anchor, good for rocky ground.

bank.question: In a UK shipping forecast, what does the term 'Backing' mean?
bank.explanation: Backing describes a wind direction change in an anti-clockwise direction (e.g., North to North-West)
options: The wind is increasing in strength (Gale warning)
The wind direction is changing in an anti-clockwise direction
The wind direction is changing in a clockwise direction
The wind is becoming light and variable

bank.question: How is an 'Estimated Position' (EP) calculated?
bank.explanation: Estimated Position (EP) accounts for the boat's movement through the water (Dead Reckoning) plus the effects of tide and wind
options: Course over ground and distance run
Dead Reckoning corrected for magnetic variation only
Dead Reckoning corrected for tidal stream and leeway
A fix obtained by GPS coordinates

bank.question: In IALA Region A, what are the characteristics of a 'Preferred Channel to Starboard' mark?
bank.explanation: A Preferred Channel to Starboard mark is red with one green horizontal band, indicating the main channel is to its starboard side (IALA A)
options: Plain green buoy with a cone topmark
Red and white vertical stripes with a single red ball
Yellow and black horizontal stripes with two cones pointing up
Red with one green horizontal band and a red cylinder (can) topmark

bank.question: When entering a harbour in the UK (IALA Region A), which port hand lateral mark should you keep to your left?
bank.explanation: On a chart, the 'Port' hand lateral mark (IALA Region A) is red, has a can shape, and a flat top.
options: A spherical mark, red and white vertical stripes.
A pillar mark, black and yellow, with cones pointing upwards.
A can-shaped mark, red, with a flat top.
A conical mark, green, with a pointed top.

bank.question: What are 'Neap Tides'?
bank.explanation: Neap tides occur when the sun and moon are at right angles to each other (at the first and last quarter moon), resulting in the smallest tidal range
options: The period between spring tides when the tidal range is at its smallest
The highest tide of the month occurring during a full moon
The maximum speed of a tidal stream in a narrow channel
A tide that occurs only during the winter months

bank.question: What occurs during the formation of an 'Occluded Front'?
bank.explanation: In an occluded front, the faster-moving cold front catches up with the warm front, lifting the warm air mass entirely off the ground
options: Cold air replaces warm air at sea level
A cold front overtakes a warm front
The wind direction remains constant for 24 hours
A high-pressure system remains stationary

bank.question: What is a 'Course to Steer' (CTS)?
bank.explanation: Course to Steer (CTS) is the compass heading calculated to compensate for the effects of both tide (set/drift) and wind (leeway)
options: The direction the boat's bow is pointing relative to the wind
A straight line drawn between the departure and arrival points
A heading calculated to allow for the effects of tidal stream and leeway
The speed at which the vessel is moving over the ground

bank.question: According to ColRegs, which day shape is displayed by a vessel Constrained By her Draught?
bank.explanation: A vessel constrained by her draught, which can only navigate within a narrow channel, displays a cylinder day shape.
options: A ball day shape.
A diamond day shape.
A cylinder day shape.
Two cones, apexes together (hourglass shape).

bank.question: According to COLREG Rule 19, how should vessels navigate in restricted visibility?
bank.explanation: Restricted visibility rules (Rule 19) apply in fog; vessels should proceed at a safe speed and be ready for immediate manoeuvre
options: The vessel on the starboard tack has right of way
There is no 'stand-on' vessel; every vessel must take action to avoid a collision
Vessels must sound one long blast every 5 minutes
The larger power-driven vessel must always stand-on

bank.question: What is the 'Rule of Twelfths' used for in navigation?
bank.explanation: The Rule of Twelfths is a rule of thumb used to estimate the height of the tide at any given hour between high and low water
options: Calculating the distance between two waypoints
Estimating the height of tide at a specific hour between high and low water
Determining the fuel consumption of a diesel engine
Predicting the speed of a tidal stream at springs

bank.question: What is an 'Occluded Front' on a weather map?
bank.explanation: An Occluded front occurs when a fast-moving cold front catches up with a warm front, lifting the warm air mass entirely off the ground
options: The boundary where a warm air mass replaces a cold air mass
A line of thunderstorms moving ahead of a low-pressure system
The centre of a high-pressure system (Anticyclone)
The weather front formed when a cold front overtakes a warm front

bank.question: Which knot is best suited for quickly securing a fender to a horizontal guard rail?
bank.explanation: A clove hitch is the standard knot for temporarily securing a line to a rail or post.
options: A Bowline.
A Clove Hitch.
A Figure-of-Eight knot.
A Round Turn and Two Half Hitches.

bank.question: What is the standard formula used to find the actual depth of water at a specific time?
bank.explanation: To calculate Depth, you must add the Charted Depth to the Height of Tide (CD + HoT = Depth)
options: Charted Depth minus Height of Tide
Height of Tide plus Charted Depth
Height of Tide minus Drying Height
Chart Datum plus Mean Sea Level

bank.question: What are the night-time lights for a vessel 'Not Under Command' (NUC)?
bank.explanation: A vessel 'not under command' (NUC) must show two all-round red lights in a vertical line to indicate it cannot manoeuvre as required
options: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line
Three all-round red lights in a vertical line
One all-round green light over one all-round white light
Two all-round white lights in a vertical line

bank.question: What is the primary difference between Lateral Marks and Cardinal Marks in IALA Region A?
bank.explanation: Lateral marks (Port/Starboard) indicate the edges of a channel, while Cardinal marks indicate the deepest or safest water relative to a point
options: Lateral marks define a channel; Cardinal marks show where the safest water lies relative to the mark
Lateral marks are only used at night; Cardinal marks are only used during the day
Lateral marks are always yellow; Cardinal marks are always green or red
There is no difference; they are used interchangeably in the UK

bank.question: When moored alongside, which line is known as the 'Stern Line' or 'Aft Breast Back' and is used to hold the back of the boat into the pontoon?
bank.explanation: The aft breast back (or stern line) runs perpendicular to the pontoon from the stern to prevent the boat moving away from the dock.
options: A line running from the bow perpendicular to the pontoon.
A line running from the stern parallel to the pontoon.
A line running from the stern perpendicular to the pontoon.
A spring line running from midships forward to the pontoon.

bank.question: What are the topmark and colour characteristics of a North Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: A North Cardinal mark is identified by two upward-pointing cones and a black-over-yellow colour scheme
options: Two cones pointing downwards; Yellow over Black
Two cones pointing towards each other; Black with a Yellow band
Two cones pointing away from each other; Yellow with a Black band
Two cones pointing upwards; Black over Yellow

bank.question: In UK hydrographic charts, what is the definition of 'Chart Datum'?
bank.explanation: Chart Datum is the level below which the tide will seldom fall; it is the reference level for all depths and drying heights on a chart
options: The average level of the sea over a 19-year period
The highest astronomical tide recorded in the last 10 years
The reference plane for all depths and drying heights on a chart
The water level exactly halfway between spring and neap tides

bank.question: In a navigation context, what is 'Deviation'?
bank.explanation: Deviation is the error caused by local magnetic fields (engines, electronics) on the specific boat the compass is mounted on
options: The difference between True North and Magnetic North
The error caused by the Earth's magnetic core
The error caused by magnetic influences on board the individual vessel
The difference between the vessel's heading and the tide

bank.question: When navigating in the Solent and needing to pass to the South of a hazard, which cardinal mark should you look for?
bank.explanation: A South Cardinal mark has two cones pointing downwards and a yellow-over-black colour scheme.
options: A mark with two cones pointing upwards and a yellow-over-black colour scheme.
A mark with two cones pointing downwards and a yellow-over-black colour scheme.
A mark with a single cone pointing upwards and a red-over-black colour scheme.
A mark with a single cone pointing downwards and a black-over-yellow colour scheme.

bank.question: According to COLREGs, what is the minimum light requirement for a sailing vessel of less than 7 metres in length?
bank.explanation: Under COLREGs Rule 25, a sailing vessel under 7m should show lights if possible, but at minimum must have an electric torch or lantern ready to prevent collision
options: She must show a masthead steaming light
She must have ready at hand an electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light
She must display a red over green all-round light at the masthead
She is not required to show any lights at all

bank.question: When a weather forecast mentions the wind is 'veering', what does this mean?
bank.explanation: Veering refers to the wind shifting in a clockwise direction (e.g., West to North-West)
options: The wind direction is shifting clockwise
The wind direction is shifting anti-clockwise
The wind speed is increasing rapidly
The wind speed is decreasing as a front passes

bank.question: On a nautical chart, what does the light description 'Oc' (Occulting) mean?
bank.explanation: An occulting light has a total duration of light longer than the total duration of darkness
options: A light where the duration of light is longer than the duration of darkness
A light where the duration of darkness is longer than the duration of light
A light that flashes only once every ten seconds
A light that changes colour between red and green

bank.question: When plotting an Estimated Position (EP), how is the vector representing the tidal stream identified?
bank.explanation: In an Estimated Position (EP) plot, the tidal set and drift is represented by a vector with three arrows.
options: A line marked with a single arrow.
A line marked with two arrows.
A line marked with three arrows.
A dotted line with no arrows.

bank.question: What is the definition of 'Departure' in coastal navigation?
bank.explanation: Departure is the east-west distance between two meridians, measured in nautical miles rather than degrees of longitude
options: The time a vessel leaves a port
The distance between two meridians of longitude expressed in nautical miles
The angle between the true course and the wind direction
The distance shown on the log at the end of a passage

bank.question: What is the topmark and light sequence for a North Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: A North Cardinal mark has two black cones pointing upwards and its light flashes rapidly or very rapidly in a continuous white sequence
options: Two black cones pointing downwards; 3 white flashes
Two black cones pointing towards each other; 9 white flashes
Two black cones base-to-base; 6 white flashes plus one long flash
Two black cones pointing upwards; continuous quick or very quick white flashes

bank.question: What is the light rhythm for a South Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: A South Cardinal mark flashes 6 quick (or ultra-quick) flashes followed by one long flash to help identify it
options: 3 Quick flashes
9 Quick flashes
6 Quick flashes followed by 1 long flash
A continuous stream of quick flashes

bank.question: What lights represent a vessel 'Not Under Command' at night?
bank.explanation: A vessel 'Not Under Command' displays two red all-round lights in a vertical line at night.
options: Two green all-round lights in a vertical line.
Two red all-round lights in a vertical line.
One red and one green all-round light in a vertical line.
One white all-round light and one red all-round light in a vertical line.

bank.question: In passage planning, what is meant by a 'Point of No Return'?
bank.explanation: The 'Point of No Return' is the last moment an entry can be safely aborted or a turn executed before conditions become too dangerous
options: The halfway point of a cross-channel passage
When the vessel runs out of fuel
The moment the tide turns against the vessel
The last position where a vessel can safely turn back or change course before a hazard

bank.question: Who is primarily responsible for the safety of everyone on board a private pleasure craft?
bank.explanation: Safety on board is the legal and moral responsibility of the Skipper at all times
options: The RNLI duty officer
The Skipper of the vessel
The most senior crew member by age
The local Harbour Master

bank.question: According to the 'Rule of Twelfths', during which hours of the tidal cycle does the greatest volume of water move?
bank.explanation: The 'Squish' or 'Rule of Thirds' suggests that the tide rises/falls roughly 50% of its range during the middle two hours (3rd and 4th hours) of the flow
options: The middle two hours (3rd and 4th hours)
The first hour of the flood
The last hour of the ebb
The period of Slack Water

bank.question: If you are approaching a wreck and need to pass to the North to remain in safe water, which cardinal mark should you look for?
bank.explanation: A North Cardinal mark has two cones pointing upwards and is black over yellow; you must pass to the north of it.
options: A mark with two cones pointing downwards and a black over yellow body.
A mark with two cones pointing upwards and a black over yellow body.
A mark with a single cone pointing upwards and a yellow over black body.
A mark with two cones pointing upwards and a yellow over black body.

bank.question: In meteorology, what defines a 'Warm Front'?
bank.explanation: A warm front occurs when warm air rises over a mass of cold air, often resulting in steady rain and a drop in barometric pressure
options: Cold air pushing under a mass of warm air
Warm air rising over a mass of cold air
Two cold air masses meeting and trapping warm air
A high-pressure system moving over the land

bank.question: What factors are used to plot a 'Dead Reckoning' (DR) position?
bank.explanation: A 'Dead Reckoning' position is calculated using only the vessel's course steered and the distance run through the water, ignoring external factors
options: Course steered and tidal stream only
Distance run and leeway only
Course steered and distance run through the water only
The position obtained by a GPS fix

bank.question: Under COLREGs, a sailing vessel is overtaking a power-driven vessel. Which one is the give-way vessel?
bank.explanation: Under Rule 13, any vessel overtaking any other shall keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken
options: The sailing vessel because it is more manoeuvrable
The vessel on the starboard side
Neither, they should both alter course to starboard
The sailing vessel must keep clear of the power-driven vessel

bank.question: What does 'Leeway' represent when calculating an Estimated Position?
bank.explanation: Leeway is the angle between the heading (the direction the boat is pointing) and the water track (the path through the water due to wind).
options: The angle between the magnetic north and true north.
The angle of the boat's heel due to wind pressure.
The angle between the heading (direction the boat is pointing) and the water track (path through the water due to wind).
The angle between the boat's speed through the water and its speed over the ground.

bank.question: In the RYA Tidal Tables, what is meant by a 'Secondary Port'?
bank.explanation: A Secondary Port is a location where tidal data is calculated by applying time and height differences to a primary reference port
options: A port for which tidal predictions are calculated by applying differences to a Primary Port
A port that only has high water data available
A small harbour that does not charge mooring fees
A port used only when the main port is blocked or inaccessible

bank.question: In tidal theory, what does the term 'Height of Tide' represent?
bank.explanation: The 'height of tide' is the vertical distance from the Chart Datum to the surface of the water at any given time
options: The distance from the seabed to the surface of the water
The vertical distance between the Chart Datum and the water's surface
The depth of water shown on a chart for a specific location
The difference in height between High Water and Low Water

bank.question: What is the topmark for an 'Isolated Danger Mark'?
bank.explanation: Isolated Danger marks are placed directly on or over a hazard and are identified by two black spheres as a topmark
options: A single red sphere
Two red spheres
Two black spheres
A yellow X shape

bank.question: Which knot is best for securing a boat to a metal ring on a harbour wall, as it does not jam and is very secure?
bank.explanation: The Round Turn and Two Half Hitches is the most secure knot for tying a boat to a ring or post under load.
options: A Clove Hitch.
A Bowline.
A Figure-of-Eight knot.
A Round Turn and Two Half Hitches.

bank.question: In the Northern Hemisphere, what is the general direction of wind flow around an area of Low Pressure?
bank.explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere, winds blow anticlockwise around a Low pressure system (Cyclone) and clockwise around a High
options: Anticlockwise and slightly inwards towards the centre
Clockwise and slightly outwards from the centre
Directly from North to South regardless of pressure
In a straight line from high pressure to low pressure

bank.question: How is a 'drying height' represented on a standard Admiralty chart?
bank.explanation: On a chart, a drying height (land visible at low tide) is indicated by an underlined figure, showing height above Chart Datum
options: An underlined figure (e.g., <u>2</u>.4)
A figure in brackets (e.g., (1.5))
A figure with a plus sign (e.g., +0.8)
A figure written in italics (e.g., 3.2)

bank.question: A 'Dead Reckoning' (DR) position is plotted using which two pieces of information?
bank.explanation: Dead Reckoning (DR) is the most basic form of navigation, using only the course steered and the distance run through the water
options: Course Steer and Speed over Ground
Course Steer and Distance Run through the water
Ground Track and Tidal Stream flow
Compass Heading and Leeway allowance

bank.question: What day shape indicates a vessel is 'Engaged in Fishing' (other than trawling)?
bank.explanation: A vessel engaged in fishing (other than trawling) displays two cones with apexes together in a vertical line.
options: A single sphere.
Two cones with apexes together in a vertical line.
Two cones with bases together in a vertical line.
A diamond shape.

bank.question: What are the colour characteristics of a 'Safe Water Mark'?
bank.explanation: A 'Safe Water Mark' indicates there is navigable water all around it and is often used as a landfall or fairway marker
options: Red and green horizontal bands
Yellow and black vertical stripes
Black and red horizontal stripes
Red and white vertical stripes

bank.question: Under COLREGs, how should two power-driven vessels act if they are meeting head-on?
bank.explanation: Rule 14 states that when two power-driven vessels are meeting on nearly reciprocal courses, each shall alter course to starboard to pass on the port side of the other
options: The larger vessel has right of way
Both vessels must stop and wait for a signal
Both vessels should alter course to port
Both vessels should alter course to starboard to pass port-to-port

bank.question: What is the most reliable way to determine if a risk of collision exists with an approaching vessel?
bank.explanation: If the bearing of an approaching vessel does not change significantly, a risk of collision is deemed to exist
options: The compass bearing of the other vessel remains constant
The other vessel appears to be getting larger very quickly
The other vessel crosses your bow from port to starboard
The other vessel shows a green sidelight to your green sidelight

bank.question: When navigating in open water, which buoy is used to mark a hazard on the chart with deep water on all sides?
bank.explanation: An Isolated Danger mark is positioned over a hazard that has navigable water all around it. It is identified by two black spheres and a red and black horizontal striped body.
options: A Lateral Mark (red cylindrical).
An Isolated Danger Mark.
A Safe Water Mark (red sphere).
A Special Mark (yellow cross).

bank.question: A vessel 'Restricted in her Ability to Manoeuvre' (RAM) must show which lights at night when making way?
bank.explanation: Under COLREGs, a 'vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre' displays a Red-White-Red vertical light sequence
options: Red over Red (Vertical)
Green over White (Vertical)
Red over White over Red (Vertical)
White over Red (Vertical)

bank.question: In what situation should you send a 'Distress' alert via a Marine VHF DSC radio?
bank.explanation: A DSC 'Distress' alert is the highest priority call and should only be used when a vessel is in grave and imminent danger
options: When the vessel has run out of fuel but is safe
To ask for a weather update from the Coastguard
When the vessel and crew are in grave and imminent danger
To inform other vessels of a floating log in the area

bank.question: How do you determine the 'Standard Time' zone used in a specific Tide Table?
bank.explanation: Standard Port time zones are listed in the Admiralty Tide Tables; UT (Universal Time) is frequently used as the base
options: By adding 1 hour to every time shown in the table
By checking the 'Time Zone' or 'Standard Time' header for that port in the tide table
By always assuming the time is GMT (UTC +0)
By correlating the table with the ship's logbook entries

bank.question: Which knot is used to tie a secure loop in the end of a line that will not slip or jam?
bank.explanation: The Bowline is the most common knot used to form a secure, fixed loop at the end of a rope that will not slip or jam under load.
options: A Reef Knot.
A Figure-of-Eight knot.
A Sheet Bend.
A Bowline.

bank.question: In the standard RYA navigation formula 'T-V-M-D-C', what does the 'C' stand for?
bank.explanation: The prefix 'C' stands for 'Correct', indicating the final heading the pilot must steer on the compass
options: Course to Steer (True)
Course Over Ground (COG)
Compass Variation Rate
Compass Heading (CH)

bank.question: What does the term 'Leeway' refer to in navigation?
bank.explanation: Leeway is the sideways drift of a vessel caused by the wind pushing against the hull and rigging
options: The drift caused by tidal streams and currents
The sideways drift of a vessel caused by the wind
The difference between Magnetic North and True North
The distance a vessel travels in one hour of sailing

bank.question: What celestial alignment causes 'Spring Tides'?
bank.explanation: Spring tides occur when the Sun and Moon are aligned, creating the greatest gravitational pull and thus the largest range
options: The Sun and Moon are at right angles to each other relative to Earth
The Sun and Moon are in line with the Earth (New or Full Moon)
The Earth is at its closest point to the Sun in its orbit
The wind is blowing in the same direction as the rising tide

bank.question: At night, what type of vessel is indicated by two all-round lights in a vertical line, where the top light is green and the bottom light is white?
bank.explanation: A vessel engaged in trawling displays a green light over a white light in a vertical line (Green over White, Trawling Night).
options: A vessel engaged in fishing
A vessel engaged in trawling
A vessel not under command
A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre

bank.question: According to COLREGs Rule 19, what action should you take when hearing a fog signal apparently forward of your beam in restricted visibility?
bank.explanation: Under Rule 19, every vessel must proceed at a safe speed. On hearing a fog signal forward of the beam, a vessel should reduce to steerage way or stop until the danger is over
options: Maintain course and speed but post an extra lookout
Reduce speed to the minimum at which the vessel can be kept on course
Alter course immediately to port to clear the other vessel
Increase speed to clear the area as quickly as possible

bank.question: What is the correct topmark for a West Cardinal buoy?
bank.explanation: A West Cardinal mark has a single yellow band on a black body, or black-yellow-black horizontal bands, and its topmark features two cones with points towards each other (in-pointing)
options: Two cones pointing upwards
Two cones pointing towards each other (points together)
Two cones pointing downwards
Two cones pointing away from each other (bases together)

bank.question: What is the topmark for a West Cardinal mark?
bank.explanation: A West Cardinal mark stays to the west of a hazard. Its topmark consists of two cones pointing towards each other (point-to-point), resembling a waist
options: Two cones pointing upwards
Two cones pointing downwards
Two cones with points together (pointing towards each other)
Two cones with bases together (pointing away from each other)

bank.question: When moored alongside a pontoon, which line prevents the boat from moving forward?
bank.explanation: The Aft Spring runs from the stern of the boat forward to the pontoon to prevent the vessel from moving forward.
options: A bow spring
A stern line
An aft spring
A breast line

bank.question: In a UK shipping forecast, what does the term 'Veering' mean?
bank.explanation: Veering refers to a clockwise shift in wind direction (e.g., West to Northwest), whereas backing refers to an anti-clockwise shift
options: A clockwise change in wind direction
An anti-clockwise change in wind direction
Wind speed increasing by more than 10 knots
A change in wind direction caused by local land effects

bank.question: Approximately how often do Spring Tides occur?
bank.explanation: Spring tides occur when the gravitational pull of the Sun and Moon are aligned, which happens shortly after every New Moon and Full Moon
options: Every New Moon and Full Moon
Only during the Summer Solstice
Once every 28 days during the first quarter moon
During the Autumnal Equinox only

bank.question: When plotting an 'Estimated Position' (EP) on a chart, which factors are added to the Dead Reckoning (DR)?
bank.explanation: An Estimated Position (EP) is the most accurate plot because it combines your intended movement (DR) with the external forces of tide (Set and Drift) and Leeway
options: Course to Steer and Tidal Stream
Dead Reckoning and Log Speed
Compass Heading and Magnetic Variation
Dead Reckoning, Tidal Stream (Set/Drift), and Leeway

bank.question: You are navigating in open water and see a hazard on the chart that has deep water on all sides. Which navigation mark indicates this type of hazard?
bank.explanation: An Isolated Danger Mark is placed over a hazard with navigable water all around it; it is identified by two black spheres.
options: A safe water mark
An isolated danger mark
A cardinal mark
A special mark

bank.question: Under COLREGs, which vessel has the highest priority and must be avoided by all others if they are able?
bank.explanation: A vessel 'Not Under Command' (NUC) is unable to manoeuvre as required by the Rules and therefore has the highest priority in the 'stand-on' hierarchy
options: A power-driven vessel
A vessel 'Not Under Command'
A vessel engaged in fishing
A sailing vessel

bank.question: Under COLREGs, when two sailing vessels have the wind on the same side, which one is the stand-on vessel?
bank.explanation: In a 'leeward' situation where two sailing vessels have the wind on the same side, the vessel which is to windward shall keep out of the way of the vessel which is to leeward
options: The larger vessel stands on
The vessel with the wind on the port side stands on
The vessel to leeward stands on
The vessel to windward stands on

bank.question: A profile view of a ship at night. It displays two vertical red lights on the mast and a green sidelight visible, indicating it is making way through the water. You see these lights at night. What type of vessel are you looking at?
bank.explanation: A vessel 'not under command' (NUC) displays two all-round red lights in a vertical line when making way through the water
options: Vessel constrained by draught
Vessel aground
Vessel not under command, making way
Vessel engaged in fishing

bank.question: According to ColRegs Rule 13, into which sector must another vessel enter for it to be considered an 'overtaking' vessel?
bank.explanation: A vessel is deemed to be overtaking when she approaches another from a direction more than 22.5 degrees abaft her beam.
options: More than 90 degrees abaft her beam
More than 22.5 degrees abaft her beam
Less than 22.5 degrees abaft her beam
Between her beam and the bow

bank.question: A pillar-shaped buoy with two black cones pointing upwards as a topmark. The buoy is painted black on top and yellow on the bottom half. Identify this buoy and the correct action to take?
bank.explanation: A North Cardinal mark has two cones pointing up, with a black-over-yellow colour scheme. Pass to the North of it
options: North Cardinal - Pass to the North
South Cardinal - Pass to the South
Isolated Danger - Pass with caution
East Cardinal - Pass to the East

bank.question: What is 'Variation' in marine navigation?
bank.explanation: Variation is the angular difference between Magnetic North and True North, caused by the Earth\'s magnetic field; it changes depending on your location and the year
options: The error caused by magnetic items on the boat
The difference between the boat's heading and its track over ground
The difference between Tide height and Chart Datum
The angular difference between True North and Magnetic North

bank.question: A large commercial vessel seen in daylight. Hanging from the rigging is a single black cylinder day shape. What does the black cylinder day shape on this vessel indicate?
bank.explanation: Large vessels in narrow channels or fairways display a cylinder day shape to indicate they are constrained by their draught
options: Vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
Vessel constrained by her draught
Vessel at anchor
Vessel engaged in towing

bank.question: Which day shape correctly indicates a vessel aground?
bank.explanation: A vessel aground must display three black balls in a vertical line during daylight hours.
options: One black ball
Two black diamonds in a vertical line
Three black balls in a vertical line
One black cylinder

bank.question: A red buoy with a flat top (can shape) floating in a channel. No topmark is present. You are entering a harbour (upstream) in the UK. On which side should you leave this mark?
bank.explanation: Single-unit lateral marks in IALA Region A use red cans for Port and green cones for Starboard when entering a harbour
options: Starboard hand mark - Leave to starboard when entering upstream
Preferred channel mark - Leave to port
Emergency wreck buoy
Port hand mark - Leave to port when entering upstream

bank.question: What is the standard unit of measurement for depth on a modern metric Admiralty Chart?
bank.explanation: Standard Admiralty charts use 'Metres' for depths and heights, with any drying heights underlined and also in metres
options: Fathoms
Metres
Feet
Cables

bank.question: A daylight view of a tug boat pulling a long barge on a hawser. Both the tug and the barge are displaying a black diamond shape. What is the meaning of the diamond day shape shown on this tow?
bank.explanation: A black diamond shape on both the tug and the tow indicates the total length of the tow exceeds 200 metres
options: Towing length is less than 100 metres
Towing vessel is restricted in its ability to manoeuvre
The length of the tow exceeds 200 metres
The vessel is carrying dangerous cargo

bank.question: Which knot is best used to join the end of a thick mooring line to a thinner heaving line?
bank.explanation: A sheet bend is the standard knot used to securely join two ropes of different diameters.
options: A reef knot
A sheet bend
A bowline
A clove hitch

bank.question: A yacht under sail with its engine running. It is displaying an inverted black cone (point down) in the forward part of the rigging. What does the inverted cone on this yacht indicate?
bank.explanation: The symbol of a yacht with an engine silhouette indicates a sailing vessel under both sail and power, which is treated as a power-driven vessel
options: The yacht is at anchor
The yacht is using machinery (engine) as well as sails
The yacht is in distress
The yacht is restricted in its ability to manoeuvre

bank.question: What characterizes an 'Occulting' (Oc) light sequence?
bank.explanation: An 'Occulting' light is a rhythmic light where the total duration of light in each period is longer than the total duration of darkness
options: The duration of light is longer than the duration of darkness
The duration of darkness is longer than the duration of light
The light has equal periods of light and darkness
The light flashes very quickly more than 50 times per minute

bank.question: A buoy with black and red horizontal stripes. The topmark consists of two black spheres positioned one above the other. What kind of navigation mark is ?
bank.explanation: An Isolated Danger mark is placed on or near a hazard with navigable water all around it; it is identifying by two black spheres
options: Isolated Danger Mark
Safe Water Mark
Special Mark
Emergency Wreck Mark

bank.question: When entering a UK harbour from the sea (IALA Region A), what is typically used as a Starboard Hand lateral mark?
bank.explanation: In IALA Region A, when returning to harbour (moving with the direction of buoyage), Starboard hand marks are green conical buoys.
options: A red can buoy
A green conical buoy
A yellow spherical buoy
A black pillar buoy

bank.question: A snippet of a nautical chart showing a drying height symbol: the number 2 with a line underneath it (<u>2</u>) located in a green tinted area. What does this underlined '2' symbol on a UK nautical chart represent?
bank.explanation: This chart symbol indicates a depth that is dry at Lowest Astronomical Tide (LAT), usually found in drying areas like mudflats
options: Depth of 2 metres at High Water
Depth of 2 metres at Chart Datum
A hazard 2 metres below the surface
Drying height of 2 metres above Chart Datum

bank.question: How do you calculate the actual depth of water at a specific time?
bank.explanation: To calculate the depth of water, you take the charted depth and add the current height of the tide for that specific time
options: Charted Depth minus Height of Tide
Charted Depth multiplied by the Rule of Twelfths
Charted Depth plus Height of Tide
Height of Tide minus Drying Height

bank.question: A large motor cruiser seen in daylight. At the front of the vessel, a single black ball is suspended from a forestay. What status does the black ball day shape indicate for this vessel?
bank.explanation: A single black ball is the international day signal for a vessel at anchor
options: Aground
At anchor
Not under command
Restricted in ability to manoeuvre

bank.question: According to ColRegs Rule 13, which vessel is the 'Give-way' vessel in an overtaking situation?
bank.explanation: Under Rule 13, any vessel approaching another from more than 22.5 degrees abaft her beam is the overtaking vessel and must keep out of the way.
options: The vessel being overtaken
The overtaking vessel
The vessel to starboard
The vessel to port

bank.question: A pillar buoy with horizontal stripes of black, then yellow in the middle, then black at the bottom. The topmark consists of two cones with their bases together. Identify this buoy and its required passing side?
bank.explanation: The East Cardinal mark has two cones pointing away from each other (base-to-base) and a black-yellow-black horizontal stripe pattern
options: West Cardinal - Pass to the West
North Cardinal - Pass to the North
East Cardinal - Pass to the East
South Cardinal - Pass to the South

bank.question: What is the primary purpose of a 'Clearing Bearing' in coastal navigation?
bank.explanation: A clearing bearing (or safety bearing) is used to ensure a vessel stays in safe water by remaining on one side of a specific compass bearing to a known landmark
options: To ensure a vessel stays away from a hazard by remaining on one side of a bearing
To find the exact distance from a lighthouse at night
To calculate the speed of the tide in a narrow channel
To determine the maximum depth of a harbour entrance

bank.question: A ship at night showing three lights in a vertical line: Red on top, White in the middle, and Red on the bottom. Sidelights are also visible. What do these vertical lights at night signify?
bank.explanation: Three vertical lights (Red-White-Red) indicate a vessel restricted in its ability to manoeuvre (RAM), such as a dredger or cable layer
options: Restricted in ability to manoeuvre
Constrained by draught
Vessel aground
Vessel engaged in pilotage duty

bank.question: Which knot is preferred for securing a line to a heavy mooring ring on a sea wall, especially when it needs to be easily undone after being heavily loaded?
bank.explanation: A Round Turn and Two Half Hitches is the preferred knot for securing a line to a heavy metal ring as it is easy to undo even after being heavily loaded.
options: A cleat hitch
A figure-of-eight knot
A round turn and two half hitches
A fisherman's bend

bank.question: A pillar buoy with vertical red and white stripes. It has a single red sphere as its topmark. Identify this navigation mark?
bank.explanation: A Safe Water Mark, often used as a fairway or landfall buoy, has vertical red and white stripes and a single red sphere topmark
options: Special Mark
Port Hand Mark
Safe Water Mark
Isolated Danger Mark

bank.question: What are the vertical 'all-round' lights for a vessel engaged in fishing (other than trawling)?
bank.explanation: A vessel engaged in fishing (but not trawling) displays a red light over a white light in a vertical line to indicate its status
options: Green over White
Red over Red
White over Red
Red over White

bank.question: A medium-sized motor vessel in daylight displaying two black balls in a vertical line where they can best be seen. What is the status of a vessel displaying these day shapes?
bank.explanation: Two black spheres indicate a vessel Not Under Command (NUC), unable to deviate from her course
options: Vessel at anchor
Vessel not under command
Vessel constrained by her draught
Vessel engaged in fishing

bank.question: You are navigating near a sandbank and need to pass to the East. Which cardinal mark indicates that safe water is to the East?
bank.explanation: The East Cardinal mark has two cones pointing away from each other (bases together) and indicates safe water is to the East.
options: A North Cardinal Mark
A South Cardinal Mark
An East Cardinal Mark
A West Cardinal Mark

bank.question: A South Cardinal buoy in the water. The top half is yellow, the bottom half is black. The topmark consists of two black cones, both pointing downwards. Identify this cardinal mark and the safe side on which to pass it?
bank.explanation: A yellow and black buoy with two cones pointing down is a South Cardinal mark; pass to the South of it
options: North Cardinal - Pass to the North
East Cardinal - Pass to the East
South Cardinal - Pass to the South
West Cardinal - Pass to the West

bank.question: What weather conditions are typically associated with the passage of a Warm Front?
bank.explanation: A warm front is typically characterized by a gradual increase in temperature, falling pressure, and steady, prolonged rain or drizzle as the front passes
options: Sudden heavy thunderstorms and a rapid rise in pressure
Steady rain or drizzle and a rise in temperature
Clear blue skies and a drop in humidity
Strong winds veering rapidly with clear visibility

bank.question: A dark night scene showing a single, bright white light on the horizon. There are no other coloured sidelights visible. At night, you see this single white light. What is the most likely source?
bank.explanation: A single white light seen from ahead on a small power-driven vessel under 7m and 7 knots is the all-round white light
options: A power-driven vessel of less than 7 metres in length
The stern of a large cargo ship
A lighthouse in the distance
A rowing boat at anchor

bank.question: Which of the following describes the shape of a West Cardinal Mark, indicating that the safest water lies to its West?
bank.explanation: A West Cardinal mark has two cones point-to-point (waist) and indicates that the safest water lies to the West.
options: Two cones pointing towards each other (waist)
Two cones pointing upwards
Two cones pointing downwards
A single spherical topmark

bank.question: A yellow pillar buoy floating in a channel. It features a yellow 'X' (St Andrew's Cross) as a topmark. What type of navigation mark is indicated by this yellow 'X' topmark?
bank.explanation: A yellow 'X' topmark indicates a Special Mark, used for features like outfalls or racing buoys
options: A safe water mark
An isolated danger mark
An emergency wreck buoy
A special mark

bank.question: Which VHF channel is used for initial Distress, Safety and Calling?
bank.explanation: Channel 16 is the international distress, safety, and calling frequency; it must be monitored by all vessels equipped with VHF
options: Channel 06
Channel 12
Channel 16
Channel 72

bank.question: Night scene showing three lights in a vertical line. The top light is red, the middle is white, and the bottom is red. side lights are not shown. What does this light configuration indicate at night?
bank.explanation: A vertical line of Red-White-Red lights indicates a vessel Restricted in her Ability to Manoeuvre (RAM)
options: A vessel engaged in pilotage duty
A vessel aground
A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
A vessel constrained by her draught

bank.question: Which of the following day shapes indicates a vessel engaged in trawling?
bank.explanation: A vessel engaged in trawling displays two cones with their apexes together (hourglass shape).
options: Two cones with their apexes together (hourglass shape)
A single black diamond shape
Three black balls in a vertical line
Two black cylinders in a vertical line

bank.question: Close up of a nautical chart showing a green area (drying bank). Inside the green area is the number 3.5 with a line underneath it. On a UK chart, what does this symbol within a green shaded area represent?
bank.explanation: A height of 3.5m underlined on a chart represents a 'drying height', which is the height above Chart Datum
options: A drying height of 3.5m above Chart Datum
A depth of 3.5m at Mean High Water Springs
A clearance of 3.5m under a bridge
A depth of 3.5m below Chart Datum

bank.question: In tidal stream terminology, what does the 'Set' refer to?
bank.explanation: The 'Set' of a tide or current refers to the direction towards which the water is moving, usually expressed in degrees True
options: The speed of the water in knots
The direction towards which the tide is flowing
The vertical distance between high and low water
The direction from which the wind is blowing

bank.question: A large ship seen in daylight. It is displaying three black spheres in a vertical line on its mast. What is the meaning of this day shape configuration?
bank.explanation: Three black balls in a vertical line indicate a vessel aground
options: A vessel engaged in mine clearance
A vessel aground
A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
A vessel at anchor

bank.question: Which knot is best suited for temporarily hanging a fender from a horizontal rail, though it can slip if used for permanent mooring?
bank.explanation: The Clove Hitch is used for temporary attachments to a rail or piling but can slip or jam if used for permanent mooring.
options: Clove Hitch
Bowline
Figure-of-Eight Knot
Sheet Bend

bank.question: A pillar buoy with horizontal black and red stripes. On top of the buoy are two black spheres arranged vertically. Which type of mark is represented by these colours and topmark?
bank.explanation: Isolated danger marks have two black spheres as a topmark and indicate hazards with navigable water all around
options: Safe Water Mark
Preferred Channel Mark
Isolated Danger Mark
Emergency Wreck Buoy

bank.question: In the RYA tidal method, what is a 'Secondary Port'?
bank.explanation: Secondary ports are calculated by applying time and height differences to the data of a designated primary port
options: A port with no tidal movement
A port where tide tables are published in full for every day
A port where tide times/heights are found by applying differences to a primary port
A port located within a locked marina system

bank.question: A snippet of a nautical chart showing a magenta dashed line snaking across the seabed, often accompanied by a small magenta telephone or lightning symbol. What does this magenta dashed line on a chart indicate?
bank.explanation: A red-white-red-white-red pattern on a chart indicates a submarine cable
options: Undersea pipeline
Submarine cable
Recommended track
Harbour limit

bank.question: After taking three visual bearings with a hand-bearing compass and plotting them on a chart, which symbol is traditionally used to represent this 'Fix'?
bank.explanation: A 'Fix' is a position derived from two or more external observations (like bearings) and is traditionally marked with a circle around a dot.
options: A circle around a dot
A square around a cross
A triangle with a dot inside
A single cross mark

bank.question: A rectangular flag with a swallow-tail. The half closer to the hoist is white, and the outer half is blue. What is the meaning of this International Code Flag?
bank.explanation: The flag 'A' (Alpha) signifies 'I have a diver down; keep well clear at slow speed.'
options: I am dragging my anchor
I require a pilot
I am carrying dangerous cargo
I have a diver down; keep well clear at slow speed

bank.question: What data must be added to a Dead Reckoning (DR) position to find an Estimated Position (EP)?
bank.explanation: Estimated Position (EP) takes the Dead Reckoning (DR) and applies the estimated effects of tidal stream and leeway
options: Dead Reckoning + Variation + Deviation
Dead Reckoning + Tidal Stream + Leeway
Ground Track + Speed Over Ground
Heading + Magnetic North Adjustment

bank.question: A buoy with vertical red and white stripes and a single red sphere as a topmark. In the background, the sun is setting. What light characteristic would you expect this buoy to have at night?
bank.explanation: A Safe Water Mark (red/white stripes) uses an occulting, isophase, or Long Flash (LFL 10s) light
options: Single long flash every 10 seconds
Quick flashing white light
Group flashing (2) every 5 seconds
Continuous red light

bank.question: When navigating at night and observing a power-driven vessel crossing from your port to starboard, which light colour represents the vessel's Starboard Sidelight?
bank.explanation: A vessel under power between 7m and 20m must show a masthead light, sidelights, and a sternlight. The green sidelight is visible on the starboard side.
options: Green
Red
White
Yellow

bank.question: A nautical chart showing an anchor symbol that has been struck through with a magenta diagonal cross. What does this symbol on a nautical chart tell the mariner?
bank.explanation: An anchor symbol with a cross through it on a chart indicates that anchoring is prohibited
options: Recommended anchorage
Deep water anchorage for tankers
Small craft mooring area
Anchoring prohibited

bank.question: Under COLREGs, which vessel has the responsibility to keep out of the way during an overtaking maneuver?
bank.explanation: Under COLREGs Rule 13, any vessel overtaking another must keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken
options: The overtaking vessel must keep out of the way
The vessel being overtaken must move to starboard
The sailing vessel always has right of way over a motor vessel
Both vessels must alter course to starboard to pass port-to-port

bank.question: A medium-sized workboat at sea displaying three black day shapes in a vertical line: a ball at the top, a diamond in the middle, and a ball at the bottom. What is the status of a vessel displaying these three vertical day shapes?
bank.explanation: The three black shapes (Ball-Diamond-Ball) indicate a vessel restricted in its ability to manoeuvre, such as one engaged in diving or underwater operations
options: Vessel at anchor
Vessel constrained by draught
Vessel restricted in ability to manoeuvre
Vessel aground

bank.question: When moored alongside in a tidal current, which line prevents the vessel from moving forward and runs from the bow of the boat aft to the pontoon?
bank.explanation: The forward spring runs from the bow of the boat aft to the pontoon, preventing the vessel from moving forward.
options: Forward Spring
After Spring
Bow Line
Stern Line

bank.question: A pillar-shaped buoy painted with red and white vertical stripes, featuring a single red sphere (ball) as a topmark. Which type of buoy is represented by this colour scheme and topmark?
bank.explanation: A white cylinder with a horizontal red band indicates a safe water mark, used to show that there is navigable water all around the mark
options: Safe Water Mark
Isolated Danger Mark
Special Mark
Emergency Wreck Buoy

bank.question: What are the colors of an 'Isolated Danger' mark?
bank.explanation: An isolated danger mark is placed directly over a hazard and is identified by two black spheres and a white flashing (2) light
options: Yellow with a black horizontal band
Red and green horizontal bands
Solid black with a yellow base
Black with one or more red horizontal bands

bank.question: A snippet of a nautical chart showing a magenta arrow with two feathers on its tail, pointing towards a coastal bay. What does this arrow symbol on a nautical chart indicate?
bank.explanation: The 'shunting' arrows (standard chart symbol) indicate the direction of the flood stream or a specific tidal flow direction
options: Prevailing wind direction
Direction of the ebb tide
Direction of the flood tide
Recommended track for small craft

bank.question: When navigating near a hazard, if a chart indicates you must stay to the South of the mark, which Cardinal mark should you look for, characterised by two cones pointing downwards and a yellow over black colour scheme?
bank.explanation: A South Cardinal mark has two cones pointing downwards and a yellow over black colour scheme. It indicates safe water is to the South.
options: South Cardinal Mark
North Cardinal Mark
East Cardinal Mark
West Cardinal Mark

bank.question: A ship at sea with two black spheres (balls) hanging vertically from its masthead or rigging. No other shapes are visible. Identifying these day shapes, what is the status of this vessel?
bank.explanation: Two black balls in a vertical line indicate a vessel 'Not Under Command', meaning it cannot deviate from its course due to exceptional circumstances like engine failure
options: Vessel at anchor
Vessel not under command
Vessel engaged in fishing
Vessel constrained by draught

bank.question: In navigation, what is a 'Fix'?
bank.explanation: A fix is the intersection of two or more position lines (LOPs) based on observed features at a specific time
options: The vessel's planned path on the chart
A position derived from at least two independent lines of position
A position calculated using only speed and time from a known point
The depth of water directly beneath the keel

bank.question: A night-time view of a horizon where two bright red lights are positioned vertically one above the other. No other navigation lights are visible. What does this light configuration signify at night?
bank.explanation: Two red lights in a vertical line signify a vessel 'Not Under Command' at night, indicating it is unable to manoeuvre as required by the ColRegs
options: Vessel at anchor
Pilot vessel on duty
Vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
Vessel not under command

bank.question: After performing a 'Running Fix' by taking two bearings of a lighthouse at different times, which symbol is used to denote the Transferred Position Line?
bank.explanation: A 'running fix' uses a transferred position line, which is traditionally marked with two arrows at each end of the line.
options: Two arrows at each end of the line
A single arrow at one end of the line
A 'T' at each end of the line
A dashed line without arrows

bank.question: A red cylindrical (can) buoy floating in a channel, with no topmark. Identify this buoy and the side on which it should be left when entering a harbour?
bank.explanation: In IALA Region A (UK), a port hand lateral mark is red, often cylindrical (can) shaped, and marks the left side of a channel when following the direction of buoyage
options: Port Hand Mark - leave to port when entering harbour
Starboard Hand Mark - leave to starboard when entering harbour
Special Mark - indicates a racing buoy
Emergency Wreck Buoy - do not pass close by

bank.question: What is the standard unit of measurement for atmospheric pressure on a UK weather map?
bank.explanation: Pressure is measured in millibars or hectopascals; 1013mb is standard, with 'high' pressure usually being above 1020mb
options: Millibars (mb) or Hectopascals (hPa)
Isobars per hour
Knots per square inch
Centimeters of Mercury (cmHg)

bank.question: A nautical chart excerpt showing the letters 'Wk' surrounded by a precise circle of small black dots or 'fringe'. What does this specific wreck symbol on a nautical chart represent?
bank.explanation: The chart symbol 'Wk' with a circle of dots indicates a wreck that is always underwater at the chart datum level
options: A wreck visible at low water
A wreck always underwater/submerged
A dangerous rock at chart datum
A designated anchoring area for fishing vessels

bank.question: Which knot is correctly used to securely fasten a rope to a deck cleat during the mooring process?
bank.explanation: The Cleat Hitch is the standard and most secure way to fasten a line to a deck cleat.
options: Cleat Hitch
Reef Knot
Round Turn and Two Half Hitches
Fisherman's Bend

bank.question: A large ship at night displaying three red lights in a vertical line, along with standard steaming lights (masthead and sidelights). What is the status of a vessel showing these three vertical red lights?
bank.explanation: Three vertical red lights indicate a vessel constrained by her draught, meaning she is severely restricted in her ability to deviate from course due to the depth of water
options: Vessel engaged in underwater cable laying
Vessel Not Under Command
Pilot vessel on duty
Vessel constrained by her draught

bank.question: What is the topmark for a 'Safe Water Mark'?
bank.explanation: A single spherical red topmark indicates a Safe Water Mark, often used to mark the start of a channel
options: Two black cones pointing downwards
A single yellow cross
A single red sphere
Two black spheres

bank.question: A cardinal buoy painted yellow on top, black in the middle, and yellow on the bottom (or yellow above black), with a topmark of two black cones pointing downwards. Identify this cardinal mark and the safe side on which to pass it?
bank.explanation: A yellow buoy with a black horizontal band and two cones pointing downwards is a South Cardinal mark; safe water lies to the South
options: North Cardinal - pass to the North
South Cardinal - pass to the South
East Cardinal - pass to the East
West Cardinal - pass to the West

bank.question: When approaching a hazard and needing to pass it on the Northern side, which Cardinal Mark should you look for, indicated by two cones pointing upwards?
bank.explanation: A North Cardinal mark has two cones pointing upwards and indicates that the safest water lies to the North of the mark.
options: North Cardinal Mark
South Cardinal Mark
East Cardinal Mark
West Cardinal Mark

bank.question: A very large crude carrier (tanker) displaying a single black cylinder (can) shape high up in its rigging. What does this black cylinder day shape indicate?
bank.explanation: A cylinder shape ('can' day shape) is the required signal for a vessel constrained by its draught during daylight hours
options: Vessel at anchor
Vessel engaged in towing
Vessel constrained by her draught
Vessel restricted in ability to manoeuvre

bank.question: When converting a 'True' bearing to a 'Magnetic' bearing, how do you apply Variation?
bank.explanation: Variation must be applied to convert a True bearing (from the chart) to a Magnetic bearing (for the compass)
options: Variation is not used for bearings
Add Westerly variation / Subtract Easterly variation
Subtract Westerly variation / Add Easterly variation
Multiply the True bearing by the annual change factor

bank.question: The International Code Flag 'Alpha', which is vertically split with white on the hoist side and blue on the fly side, featuring a swallow-tail cut. What is the meaning of this International Code Flag when flown by a vessel?
bank.explanation: The blue and white 'Alpha' flag is the international signal indicating that the vessel has a diver down and other vessels should keep well clear at slow speed
options: I have a diver down; keep well clear at slow speed
I am taking in or discharging explosives
I am dragging my anchor
My vessel is healthy and I request free pratique

bank.question: Which light configuration indicates a vessel engaged in trawling at night?
bank.explanation: A vessel engaged in trawling shows a green light over a white light. A useful memory aid is: 'Green over white, trawling by night'.
options: A green light over a white light
A red light over a white light
A white light over a green light
A white light over a red light

bank.question: A West Cardinal pillar buoy: yellow with a single broad black horizontal band in the middle, and a topmark of two black cones with points facing each other. Identify this buoy and the direction of safe water?
bank.explanation: A yellow buoy with a single horizontal black band and two cones with points together (middle) is a West Cardinal mark. Pass it to the West
options: East Cardinal - pass to the East
North Cardinal - pass to the North
West Cardinal - pass to the West
Isolated Danger - pass well clear on either side

bank.question: What are the day-shapes or lights for a vessel 'Not Under Command'?
bank.explanation: A vessel 'not under command' (NUC) must display two all-round red lights in a vertical line when making way
options: Two green lights in a vertical line
Three red lights in a vertical line
One white light over one red light
Two red lights in a vertical line

bank.question: A yellow pillar-shaped buoy with a single yellow 'X' shaped topmark (St Andrew's Cross). Identify the type of buoy shown?
bank.explanation: A yellow cross topmark on a yellow buoy identifies it as a Special Mark, used to indicate features like outfalls or racing marks
options: Lateral Mark
Special Mark
Safe Water Mark
Emergency Wreck Buoy

bank.question: When sailing into a UK marina, what is the 'Topmark' shape that identifies the Starboard side of the channel?
bank.explanation: In IALA Region A (UK), the Port Hand mark is red and cylindrical, while the Starboard Hand mark is green and conical. Therefore, a cone shape identifies the Starboard side.
options: A cone shape
A cylinder shape
A sphere shape
A cross shape

bank.question: A sailing yacht at anchor in a bay, with a single black spherical day shape hanging from the forestay. What is the status of a vessel displaying this day shape?
bank.explanation: A vessel displaying a single black ball is at anchor. Vessels under 7m are generally exempt unless in a narrow channel
options: Vessel at anchor
Vessel aground
Vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
Vessel constrained by her draft

bank.question: In tidal stream terminology, what does the 'Drift' refer to?
bank.explanation: The 'Drift' refers to the distance (speed) the tidal stream moves in a specific direction over time
options: The speed of the tidal stream (usually in knots)
The compass direction in which the tide is flowing
The depth of the water at high tide
The distance the boat slides sideways due to wind

bank.question: A motor vessel displaying two black spherical day shapes positioned vertically one above the other. What does this day shape configuration indicate?
bank.explanation: Two black spheres in a vertical line indicate a vessel that is 'Not Under Command' due to an exceptional circumstance
options: Restricted in ability to manoeuvre
Constrained by draft
Not under command
Vessel aground

bank.question: When returning to a UK port from the sea, which shape represents the Port Hand lateral mark?
bank.explanation: In IALA Region A (UK), the Port Hand lateral mark is a red can. A helpful memory cue is: 'is there any red port left in the can?'
options: A red can
A green cone
A yellow spear
A black pillar

bank.question: A cardinal buoy with black on the top half and yellow on the bottom half. The topmark consists of two black cones, both pointing upwards. Identify this cardinal mark and the safe side on which to pass it?
bank.explanation: A North Cardinal mark is black over yellow with both cones pointing upwards. Pass to the North of this mark
options: East Cardinal - Pass East
South Cardinal - Pass South
West Cardinal - Pass West
North Cardinal - Pass North

bank.question: What is the length of one Nautical Mile?
bank.explanation: 1 nautical mile is 1.852 km; it is also defined as one minute of latitude
options: 1,000 Meters
5,280 Feet
1,852 Meters (one minute of latitude)
2,000 Yards

bank.question: An extract of a nautical chart showing a rock symbol (an asterisk shape) with the number 2.4 printed next to it, where the 4 is smaller and underlined. On a UK chart, what does this symbol and number indicate?
bank.explanation: The number 2.4 under a line signifies the drying height of the rock, meaning it is 2.4m above the Chart Datum
options: A drying height of 2.4m above Chart Datum
A depth of 2.4m at Mean High Water Springs
A rock with 2.4m of water over it at Low Water
The height of the rock above the seabed is 2.4m

bank.question: Which mooring line is specifically used as a 'Bow Line' to prevent a vessel from moving astern when moored alongside a pontoon?
bank.explanation: The bow line prevents the vessel from moving backwards (astern) and also keeps the bow close to the pontoon.
options: A line running from the bow forward to the pontoon
A line running from the stern aft to the pontoon
A line running from the midships to the pontoon
A line running from the stern forward to the pontoon

bank.question: A night-time view showing three vertical lights on a mast in the configuration: Red (top), White (middle), Red (bottom). What does this light configuration indicate at night?
bank.explanation: A vessel 'Restricted in her Ability to Manoeuvre' (RAM) shows a red-white-red vertical light sequence at night
options: Vessel at anchor
Pilot vessel on duty
Vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
Vessel engaged in fishing

bank.question: According to COLREGs, how should two power vessels meeting head-on avoid a collision?
bank.explanation: Rule 14 states that when two power-driven vessels meet head-on, both should alter course to starboard
options: Turn to port and pass starboard-to-starboard
Stay the course and sound five short blasts
Maintain speed but alter course to starboard to pass port-to-port
The larger vessel has the right of way

bank.question: A red pillar buoy with a flat-topped red cylinder (can) topmark. Identify this buoy and how you should pass it when entering a harbour?
bank.explanation: In IALA Region A (UK), a port hand lateral mark is red and has a flat 'can' topmark. Keep it to your port side when entering
options: Starboard hand mark - leave to starboard when entering harbour
Port hand mark - leave to port when entering harbour
Starboard hand mark - leave to port when entering harbour
Port hand mark - leave to starboard when entering harbour

bank.question: Which knot creates a secure loop at the end of a line that will not slip under load?
bank.explanation: A bowline forms a fixed, non-slipping loop at the end of a rope, which is essential for safety and utility on a boat.
options: A Bowline
A Reef Knot
A Clove Hitch
A Figure-of-Eight Knot

bank.question: A nautical chart snippet showing the abbreviation 'Cy' near a depth sounding. What does the abbreviation 'Cy' on a nautical chart mean regarding the seabed?
bank.explanation: The 'TBY' letters indicate the seabed is composed of 'Tiny' (T) shell and 'By' (Bly) or in standard abbreviations, 'T' is not common but 'Sh' is shell; specifically 'Cy' is Clay. In RYA terms, 'Cy' stands for Clay
options: Crystals
Clay
Coarse sand
Cinders

bank.question: In the Northern Hemisphere, what is the general direction of wind circulation around an Anticyclone (High Pressure)?
bank.explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere, winds circulate clockwise around a high-pressure system (anticyclone)
